title: 15 Best Japanese Podcasts (2026) | Beginner to Native
text: 15 Best Japanese Podcasts by Level (2026) Key Takeaways Last checked: August 2026. Podcast availability, transcripts, memberships, and episode formats can change. This post contains affiliate links. If you sign up through my link, I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Japanese podcasts are one of the easiest ways to move from textbook Japanese into the language… August 13, 2026 Japanese Key Takeaways Best for beginners: Nihongo con Teppei for Beginners Best for Genki learners: Japanese with Shun Best for intermediate learners: YUYU の日本語 Podcast Best bridge into natural conversation: The Miku Real Japanese Podcast Best native podcast for casual Japanese: となりの雑談 Best for advanced learners who love history: COTEN RADIO Last checked: August 2026. Podcast availability, transcripts, memberships, and episode formats can change. This post contains affiliate links. If you sign up through my link, I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Japanese podcasts are one of the easiest ways to move from textbook Japanese into the language you actually hear. You start noticing pacing, fillers, sentence endings, pronunciation, and everyday vocabulary that rarely fit neatly into a grammar exercise. The harder part is choosing the right podcast. Beginner audio can feel painfully controlled once your listening improves. Native podcasts can have the opposite problem: they sound interesting, but if you are only catching isolated words, an hour of listening can turn into background noise. I sorted these 15 Japanese podcasts by level, naturalness, study support, and the kind of listening practice they do best. You do not need to listen to all of them. The goal is to find the one that fits where your Japanese is right now . Quick Picks: Which Japanese Podcast Should You Start With? If you… Start with Why Are new to Japanese-only listening Nihongo con Teppei for Beginners Short, manageable Japanese-first immersion Are studying Genki Japanese with Shun Familiar N5–N4 grammar in spoken Japanese Still want English explanations Learn Japanese Pod Dialogue plus guided explanations Are moving beyond beginner material The Miku Real Japanese Podcast Natural conversation without jumping straight into native media Want more complex topics with English support Bilingual News Japanese and English in the same conversation Want regular intermediate immersion YUYU の日本語 Podcast Natural Japanese across everyday and cultural topics Want formal Japanese NHK Radio News Broadcast pronunciation and news vocabulary Love technology Rebuild.fm Native Japanese about software and tech Want real casual conversation となりの雑談 Unscripted conversation made for native listeners Love history COTEN RADIO Engaging native-level discussions about history Want JLPT-based listening Let’s Talk in Japanese! Episodes labeled from N5 to N1 My rule: choose by level first, then interest. A podcast you can follow and want to replay will usually teach you more than a harder one you keep abandoning. You do not need five podcasts at once. Pick one that matches your level, listen long enough to get used to the host, and add another only when you want a different kind of Japanese. How I Evaluate Japanese Podcasts I do not choose Japanese podcasts based on popularity alone. A useful podcast needs to work as something you can realistically return to, not just something that looks impressive in a resource list. These are the five things I pay the most attention to: Comprehensibility: Can you follow the main idea without decoding every sentence? Naturalness: Does the Japanese sound useful outside a textbook? Replay value: Is the audio clear and interesting enough to listen to again? Study support: Can you check transcripts, subtitles, vocabulary, or other material when you need it? Staying power: Is there enough interesting content to make listening part of a real routine? A beginner podcast may sacrifice some natural speed for comprehensibility. A native podcast may give you extremely natural Japanese with almost no learner support. That is why I would not try to name one universal “best” Japanese podcast. The better question is: which podcast gives you the right amount of difficulty now? Best Japanese Podcasts for Beginners The best beginner Japanese podcast should give you enough real Japanese to train your ear without making every sentence feel like a test. These three take different approaches. Teppei gives you Japanese-first immersion, Shun connects listening to familiar textbook grammar, and Learn Japanese Pod gives you more English support when you still need it. 1. Nihongo con Teppei for Beginners ↗ Level: Beginner Speed: Slow Format: Monologue Japanese: Mostly Japanese Episode Length: Short Transcript: Paid AI transcripts via Patreon Naturalness: ★★★★☆ Best for: First Japanese-first immersion Learning Value: ★★★★★ Nihongo con Teppei is one of the easiest places to start if you want to spend a few minutes entirely inside Japanese. Teppei keeps the topics familiar and the language manageable, but the episodes do not feel like traditional grammar recordings. He repeats vocabulary and ideas naturally as he talks, which gives you several chances to catch the meaning without stopping every few seconds. That repetition matters at the beginner stage. A sentence pattern you have studied on paper can appear again and again until you begin recognizing it as sound rather than mentally rebuilding the grammar every time. The beginner series also has a huge archive, so it works particularly well as a daily listening habit. If you want to check what you missed afterwards, additional transcript support is available through Patreon. The main tradeoff is that there is not much English scaffolding. If you want someone to stop and explain why an expression works, Learn Japanese Pod will feel easier. Start here if: you already know some basic Japanese and want to become comfortable listening without reaching for English every few seconds. 2. Japanese with Shun ↗ Level: Beginner–Lower Intermediate · N5–N4 Speed: Slow to moderate Format: Mostly monologue Japanese: Japanese Episode Length: Around 10–15 min Transcript: Patreon transcripts Naturalness: ★★★★☆ Best for: Genki learners Learning Value: ★★★★★ Japanese with Shun is the podcast I would pair with Genki 1 or Genki 2 . Much of Shun’s beginner content uses grammar that should already feel familiar if you are working through Genki. That creates a useful bridge between studying grammar and actually hearing it . Instead of meeting a grammar pattern once in a textbook dialogue, you hear the same structures while someone talks about travel, hobbies, daily life, food, and other ordinary topics. You already understand much of the grammar, so more of your attention can go toward listening. Episodes are also short enough to replay without turning your listening session into a major study project. Transcripts can help when you want to check what you missed or shadow a short section. The podcast will eventually become too comfortable, and that is a good thing. When you can follow most episodes without much effort, move toward Miku, YUYU, or another podcast with less controlled speech. Start here if: you use Genki and want the Japanese in your textbook to start sounding like a language people actually speak. 3. Learn Japanese Pod ↗ Level: Beginner–Lower Intermediate Speed: Slow to moderate Format: Dialogue + explanation Japanese: Japanese + English Episode Length: Varies Transcript: Show notes and additional study material Naturalness: ★★★★☆ Best for: Learners who still want explanations Learning Value: ★★★★☆ Learn Japanese Pod is the most guided option in this beginner group. Episodes are built around practical spoken Japanese and often combine dialogue with explanations of vocabulary, expressions, grammar, and cultural context. The topics focus heavily on situations and expressions you could actually encounter in everyday life. That makes it useful when Japanese-only audio still feels frustrating. You can understand what an expression means first, then return to the dialogue and hear it again with more context. The tradeoff is that the more time an episode spends explaining Japanese in English, the less uninterrupted Japanese you hear. I would use this when you need the support, then gradually add Teppei or Shun as you become more comfortable staying inside Japanese. Start here if: you want useful everyday expressions but are not ready to give up English explanations yet. Best Japanese Podcasts for Intermediate Learners Intermediate listening is where Japanese podcasts become much more interesting. You no longer need every sentence slowed down, but completely native content can still be exhausting. This stage is about getting used to longer sentences, less predictable vocabulary, natural fillers, and speakers who are no longer waiting for you to catch up. 4. The Miku Real Japanese Podcast ↗ Level: Intermediate · Around N3+ Speed: Moderate to natural Format: Monologue + conversation Japanese: Mostly Japanese Episode Length: Often around 15–35 min Transcript: Paid transcripts with furigana Naturalness: ★★★★★ Best for: Moving into natural conversation Learning Value: ★★★★★ Miku is a strong next step when beginner podcasts start feeling too controlled. The episodes move beyond grammar-syllabus topics and into conversation, culture, relationships, personal experiences, and everyday Japanese. You begin following the speaker because of what she is saying, while the language learning happens inside that experience. That is an important shift at intermediate level. Miku also offers transcript support, which is particularly useful for the classic intermediate problem: you understand a sentence immediately when you read it, but somehow did not hear it at all. Use the transcript after listening, not before. The gap between what you can read and what you can recognize by ear tells you exactly what needs more listening practice. Start here if: beginner podcasts feel too easy, but fully native conversations still move a little too quickly. 5. Bilingual News ↗ Level: Intermediate–Upper Intermediate Speed: Natural Format: Unscripted bilingual conversation Japanese: Japanese + English Episode Length: Long-form Transcript: Official transcript support Naturalness: ★★★★★ Best for: Complex topics with an English safety net Learning Value: ★★★★☆ Bilingual News works differently from almost everything else on this list. Mami and Michael discuss news, science, technology, society, and other interesting topics using both Japanese and English. The English can either help you or make you lazy. If you automatically wait for the English whenever the Japanese becomes difficult, you lose much of the listening benefit. A better approach is to process the Japanese first, make a quick guess about the meaning, and then use the English as confirmation. The topics are also more complex than the everyday themes common in learner podcasts. That means you begin hearing Japanese used for ideas that require more abstract vocabulary. It is not my first choice for pure Japanese immersion. It is one of the most useful formats for stepping into harder subject matter without completely losing the thread. Start here if: everyday learner topics are getting repetitive and you want more intellectually interesting listening without going Japanese-only yet. 6. Nihongo con Teppei 波! ↗ Level: Intermediate–Advanced Speed: Moderate to natural Format: Monologue Japanese: Japanese only Episode Length: Often around 10–30 min Transcript: Limited learner support Naturalness: ★★★★★ Best for: Frequent conversational immersion Learning Value: ★★★★★ If you started with Teppei’s beginner series, 波! feels like a natural next stage. The basic idea stays familiar: one person talking directly to you in Japanese. The difference is that the episodes are longer, the language is less restricted, and the conversation wanders more freely. That unpredictability is useful. Real listening rarely arrives in a carefully arranged order where today’s vocabulary happens to match the chapter you studied yesterday. Following one person across ordinary topics teaches you how to stay with Japanese even when you cannot predict what comes next. There is less hand-holding here than with Miku. I would treat 波! primarily as a listening habit , not a transcript-first study resource. Start here if: you already like Teppei’s style and want more natural Japanese without changing to a completely unfamiliar host. 7. YUYU の日本語 Podcast ↗ Level: Intermediate–Upper Intermediate Speed: Moderate to natural Format: Monologue + occasional conversation Japanese: Japanese Episode Length: Often around 35–50 min Transcript: Patreon support and member content Naturalness: ★★★★★ Best for: Natural intermediate immersion Learning Value: ★★★★★ YUYU is one of the strongest intermediate Japanese podcasts on this list. He talks about language learning, culture, daily life, opinions, personal experiences, and whatever catches his interest. The reason it works so well at intermediate level is that it does not feel aggressively simplified. You hear a real personality, digressions, humor, repeated ideas, and the kind of pacing that starts preparing you for native content. At the same time, YUYU is speaking to Japanese learners, so the experience is much less punishing than jumping directly into a random native radio show. The longer episodes are also useful for building listening stamina. You do not have to “study” every YUYU episode. Sometimes the best use is simply listening while walking and seeing how long you can remain mentally inside Japanese. Start here if: you want learner-friendly Japanese that no longer feels like a classroom exercise. Best Native Japanese Podcasts for Advanced Learners At advanced level, I would stop looking only for podcasts designed for Japanese learners. Native podcasts expose you to different registers, incomplete sentences, shared cultural assumptions, jokes, specialized vocabulary, interruptions, and ideas that speakers do not pause to explain. That is exactly what makes them useful. 8. NHK Radio News ↗ Level: Advanced · N2–N1 Speed: Natural broadcast speed Format: News Japanese: Japanese only Episode Length: Varies by bulletin Transcript: Related written news available separately Naturalness: ★★★★★ Best for: Formal Japanese and news vocabulary Learning Value: ★★★★☆ NHK Radio News changes the type of Japanese you are listening to. Instead of casual conversation, you hear polished broadcast pronunciation, formal vocabulary, dense information, numbers, names, and sentence structures associated with news reporting. News Japanese is its own register. Words and structures that feel unusual in casual conversation suddenly become normal when the speaker is reporting an election, economic figures, a natural disaster, or an international event. I would not use it as my only advanced podcast. The pronunciation is clear, but the information density can make it surprisingly difficult. A useful method is to choose one story, listen once, then find written Japanese coverage of the same event. If you like learning through Japanese news, I also tested Todaii Japanese , which gives you another way to work with news vocabulary and reading. Once you already understand the context, unknown vocabulary becomes much easier to infer. Start here if: conversational Japanese is comfortable and you want to strengthen formal listening for N2, N1, news, or professional contexts. 9. Rebuild.fm ↗ Level: Advanced Speed: Native Format: Host + guest conversation Japanese: Mostly Japanese Episode Length: Often 1–2+ hours Transcript: No learner transcript system Naturalness: ★★★★★ Best for: Tech, software, and internet vocabulary Learning Value: ★★★★☆ Rebuild is not a Japanese-learning podcast. That is the reason it belongs here. The show focuses on software development, technology, gadgets, and internet culture. The conversations can be long, which makes Rebuild much closer to joining a real tech conversation than completing a listening lesson. You will hear shorthand, English technical vocabulary embedded inside Japanese, casual interruptions, references that are never explained, and speakers assuming you already know what the industry is talking about. That sounds difficult, but subject knowledge changes everything. If you already understand software or AI in English, you are not learning the concept and the Japanese at the same time. You can use what you already know about the topic to predict meaning. This is one of the best ways to start building domain-specific Japanese . Start here if: technology is already something you would happily listen to for an hour even if language learning were not the goal. 10. Let’s Learn Japanese from Small Talk ↗ Level: Upper Intermediate–Advanced Speed: Natural Format: Two-person conversation Japanese: Japanese Episode Length: Often around 25–55 min Transcript: Vocabulary lists Naturalness: ★★★★★ Best for: Everyday casual conversation Learning Value: ★★★★★ Let’s Learn Japanese from Small Talk gives you something formal listening cannot: the slightly messy rhythm of real conversation. The hosts talk about daily life, travel, anime, personal experiences, feelings, and random things that come up. Vocabulary lists also make it easier to check the words that mattered in a particular conversation without relying on a full line-by-line transcript. You hear features that disappear from textbook dialogues: filler expressions, casual reactions, changing sentence endings, laughter, unfinished thoughts, and the small phrases people use to hold a conversation together. That kind of Japanese is difficult to “study” as a grammar chapter. You have to hear it repeatedly. Start here if: you understand clean learner Japanese but still struggle when two Japanese speakers relax and talk normally to each other. 11. COTEN RADIO ↗ Level: Advanced Speed: Native Format: Multi-host discussion Japanese: Japanese only Episode Length: Around 40 min for many main episodes Transcript: No learner transcript system Naturalness: ★★★★★ Best for: History, society, and big ideas Learning Value: ★★★★☆ COTEN RADIO is where “study content” starts becoming something you would listen to because the subject itself is interesting. The show explores Japanese and world history through conversations that use historical events to think about people, society, and the problems humans keep repeating. The Japanese is demanding. You will encounter historical names, abstract nouns, specialized vocabulary, jokes, reactions, and long stretches of native conversation. But the narrative structure of history can actually help: once you understand who the people are and what is happening, the language becomes easier to predict. I would not pause for every unknown historical term. Understand the story first, then go back only if a word keeps appearing or seems essential. Start here if: you are already comfortable with Japanese podcasts and want native content you would genuinely choose for the subject, not just for language practice. 12. お互いさまっす ↗ Level: Advanced Speed: Native Format: Two-person conversation Japanese: Japanese only Episode Length: Often around 15–20 min Transcript: No learner transcript system Naturalness: ★★★★★ Best for: Emotional expression and reactions Learning Value: ★★★★★ お互いさまっす is built around conversations about feelings and everyday experiences. Listeners send in stories about things that irritated them, embarrassed them, made them happy, or left them unsure what to think. The hosts respond by empathizing, imagining, joking, and connecting those stories to their own lives. For a learner, the interesting part is the emotional Japanese . Textbooks are quite good at teaching you how to ask where the station is. They are much worse at teaching the dozens of tiny ways people show hesitation, agreement, disbelief, sympathy, embarrassment, or “I know exactly what you mean.” This podcast is full of that language. The shorter episode length also makes replaying one complete native conversation much more realistic. Start here if: you want to understand how Japanese speakers react to one another, not just the dictionary meaning of the words they say. 13. となりの雑談 ↗ Level: Advanced Speed: Native Format: Unscripted conversation Japanese: Japanese only Episode Length: Around 15–20 min Transcript: No learner transcript system Naturalness: ★★★★★ Best for: Relaxed native conversation Learning Value: ★★★★★ となりの雑談 is one of the best examples of what advanced listening eventually needs to become. The idea feels a little like overhearing two interesting people talking at the table next to you. Topics move naturally from work to relationships to ageing to something that happened that week, then drift somewhere else entirely. There is no learner-friendly setup telling you today’s vocabulary before the conversation begins. What makes it difficult is not necessarily rare vocabulary. It is how much meaning is carried through context, tone, shared assumptions, sentence fragments, and things that never need to be explicitly said between two native speakers. That is exactly why it is useful. At some point, advanced listening stops being about “Can I hear every word?” and becomes “Can I stay inside the conversation even when not everything is spelled out?” Start here if: you want native conversation that feels like sitting near two interesting people and quietly listening in. Japanese Podcasts That Work Across Multiple Levels Not every podcast fits neatly into Beginner, Intermediate, or Advanced. These last two are useful because the content itself is organized by level, so you can stay with the same resource while changing the difficulty. 14. JapanesePod101 ↗ Level: Beginner–Advanced Speed: Controlled by lesson level Format: Structured audio + video lessons Japanese: Japanese + English Episode Length: Usually short lesson format Transcript: Lesson notes and paid study tools Naturalness: ★★★☆☆ Best for: Structured audio learning Learning Value: ★★★★☆ JapanesePod101 is less like an independent podcast and more like a large audio-based Japanese course. Its library combines audio and video lessons across different levels, with conversations, vocabulary, lesson notes, and additional learning tools. That structure can be either its biggest strength or its biggest weakness. If you like following your curiosity and jumping between native resources, it may feel too organized. If you constantly waste time wondering what to study next, the structure is useful. I would not choose JapanesePod101 over YUYU or となりの雑談 for pure immersion. I would choose it when I wanted someone else to organize what comes next . Start here if: you want podcast-style learning but prefer a curriculum to a feed of unrelated episodes. 15. Let’s Talk in Japanese! ↗ Level: N5–N1 Speed: Changes by level Format: Monologue Japanese: Japanese Episode Length: Usually short Transcript: Scripts/support available for members Naturalness: ★★★★☆ Best for: JLPT-leveled listening Learning Value: ★★★★★ Let’s Talk in Japanese! solves one of the most annoying problems with podcast learning: guessing whether an episode is actually at your level. Japanese teacher Tomo labels episodes from N5 to N1 to indicate approximate JLPT difficulty. That makes it especially useful when you are between levels. You can listen to an N4 episode and notice that it feels easy, try N3, and immediately get a rough sense of where your listening ability begins to break down. The topics are varied enough that it does not feel like listening to JLPT practice questions. You are still hearing someone talk about ordinary subjects in Japanese; the level label simply removes some of the trial and error. I would use the labels as guidance rather than treating them as a precise test of your JLPT ability. Podcast comprehension and JLPT listening are related, but they are not exactly the same skill. Start here if: you want a simple way to increase listening difficulty gradually without constantly changing podcasts. Best Japanese News Podcasts If you want to use Japanese news podcasts for listening practice, I would start with Bilingual News or NHK Radio News. They work for different stages, so the better choice depends on how much support you still need. Podcast Best for Level Language Bilingual News News and complex topics with English support Intermediate–Upper Intermediate Japanese + English NHK Radio News Formal news Japanese at natural broadcast speed N2–N1 Japanese Bilingual News is the easier bridge if Japanese-only news still feels too dense. Once you can follow formal Japanese more comfortably, NHK Radio News gives you clearer practice with broadcast pronunciation, current affairs vocabulary, numbers, and information-heavy sentences. You can find my full notes on both podcasts in the level-based recommendations above. Best Japanese Podcasts With Transcripts A Japanese podcast with a transcript is especially useful when you can follow the general meaning but keep missing words you already know. Listen first, then use the text to check what your ears failed to recognize. Podcast Level Transcript support Nihongo con Teppei for Beginners Beginner Paid AI transcripts via Patreon Japanese with Shun N5–N4 Patreon transcripts The Miku Real Japanese Podcast Around N3+ Paid transcripts with furigana Bilingual News Intermediate–Upper Intermediate Official transcript support YUYU の日本語 Podcast Intermediate–Upper Intermediate Patreon/member support Let’s Talk in Japanese! N5–N1 Member scripts/support I would still listen before opening the transcript . The useful moment is when you discover, “I know this sentence when I read it, but I did not recognize it when I heard it.” How to Actually Learn Japanese With Podcasts You do not need to turn every podcast episode into a two-hour study session. Most of the time, I would rather listen consistently and study one small section well than spend so long analyzing a single episode that I stop enjoying podcasts altogether. Step 1. Listen Without the Transcript Play the episode once without reading. Do not stop every time you miss a word. Listen for the topic, mood, words you recognize, repeated phrases, and the general direction of what the speaker is saying. Your first listen is a test of what your ears can already process. Step 2. Check What You Missed Listen again with the transcript, subtitles, vocabulary list, or episode notes if they are available. This is where you notice the difference between: “I don’t know this Japanese.” and: “I know this sentence. I just didn’t recognize it when someone said it.” That second problem is exactly what listening practice can fix. You can also shadow a short section by repeating the speaker aloud and trying to match the timing, pauses, and rhythm. Thirty seconds of careful imitation is often enough. Step 3. Save One Useful Sentence Do not save every unknown word. A podcast can contain dozens of unfamiliar expressions, and collecting all of them usually creates a vocabulary list you never review. Instead, choose one sentence you genuinely want to understand, remember, or use. Look at how the words work together, not just what each individual word means. Step 4. Retell What You Heard Close the transcript and explain the episode in three or four Japanese sentences. You can answer simple questions: What was the episode about? What happened? What did the speaker think? What did you find interesting? Your Japanese does not have to be perfect. The point is to discover which language you can recognize and which language you can actually produce . When I Want More Support Than Audio Alone Podcasts are great for training your ear, but there are times when I want more visual context—especially when I can hear a phrase but cannot quite work out what I am hearing. That is where I use Lingopie . Study Japanese with Lingopie → Instead of working with audio alone, you learn through shows and videos with interactive subtitles. You can check a word while you are watching, save useful vocabulary, return to it later, and replay lines when you want to listen or shadow more carefully. What I like about this workflow is that it keeps the language connected to a real scene. I do not need to turn every line into a flashcard. I can keep watching, look up the words that actually matter, save a few of them, and hear them again in context. For me, podcasts and video do different jobs: Podcasts build listening stamina. Video gives me more context when I need help understanding what I hear. Japanese Podcasts FAQs What is the best beginner Japanese podcast? For Japanese-only listening, I would start with Nihongo con Teppei for Beginners . The episodes are short, the language is manageable, and repetition makes it easier to keep following even when you miss individual words. If you are studying Genki, Japanese with Shun may be an even better fit because much of the language stays close to familiar beginner grammar. What is the best Japanese podcast for intermediate learners? My first choices are The Miku Real Japanese Podcast and YUYU の日本語 Podcast . Miku is especially good when you are first moving out of controlled beginner content. YUYU is my pick when you want longer, more natural Japanese that still feels accessible to language learners. What Japanese podcasts are good for N3? Start with Miku, YUYU, or Nihongo con Teppei 波!. At N3, I would look for material where you can understand the overall message without needing to read every line. You should still encounter enough unfamiliar vocabulary and natural speech to have something to learn. What Japanese podcasts are good for N2 or N1? At N2–N1, begin mixing learner podcasts with content made for native speakers. NHK Radio News is useful for formal Japanese, Rebuild for technology, COTEN RADIO for history, and となりの雑談 or お互いさまっす for conversational Japanese. Do I need a transcript to learn Japanese from podcasts? No. For easier material, listening without text is valuable because it forces your brain to process Japanese as sound. Transcripts become particularly useful when you can understand the general meaning but want to identify exactly what you missed. I would usually listen first and read second. Should beginners listen to native Japanese podcasts? You can, especially if you enjoy them, but I would not make them your main study material. If nearly everything sounds like an uninterrupted stream of noise, there is not enough comprehensible language for you to notice patterns easily. Keep native podcasts as optional exposure and use something easier for focused practice. How much of a Japanese podcast should I understand? There is no perfect percentage. For active study, I prefer material where I can follow the overall conversation and catch a large amount of the language, while still meeting new expressions. If you are constantly lost, move down a level. If nothing makes you think anymore, move up. How often should I listen to Japanese podcasts? Consistency matters more than long sessions. Ten or twenty focused minutes on most days can do more for your listening than one huge session followed by a week without Japanese. Replaying the same episode is also more useful than it may feel, because the second listen lets you notice language that disappeared the first time. Can Japanese podcasts help with the JLPT? Yes, especially for listening comprehension, vocabulary recognition, and getting faster at processing spoken Japanese. For more targeted practice, Let’s Talk in Japanese! is convenient because episodes are organized around different JLPT levels. Final Thoughts The best Japanese podcast is not necessarily the fastest, most native, or most popular one. It is the one you understand well enough to stay engaged with and enjoy enough to come back to. If you are a beginner, start with Teppei or Shun. If you are somewhere around intermediate, move into Miku, YUYU, or 波!. Once those begin to feel comfortable, choose native content based on what you genuinely care about—technology, history, news, relationships, or simply listening to people talk. Then keep the study process small: Listen → check → save one thing → say something back. That is enough to turn a podcast from background audio into real Japanese practice. title: jpdb vs Anki for Japanese: Media Decks or Custom Cards?
text: jpdb vs Anki for Japanese: Media Decks or Custom Flashcards? Choosing between media vocabulary decks and custom flashcards? Compare the workflows, learner tradeoffs, and migration questions before changing your Japanese reviews. October 22, 2026 Japanese Choose jpdb if you want Japanese vocabulary study organized around the books and shows you hope to understand. Choose Anki if you want to build and control your own flashcards, including their content and presentation. If your current reviews feel exhausting, identify what makes them exhausting before moving your entire vocabulary history. Both can support vocabulary practice. The more useful question is which one leaves you willing to review—and with enough time left to read and listen to Japanese. This comparison draws on official product information and linked learner discussions checked on October 22, 2026. It is a research-based guide, not an account of completing either system or a controlled learning test. jpdb vs Anki at a glance Your priority Start by considering Why Vocabulary from a particular Japanese book or show jpdb Its official site offers media vocabulary decks and tracks known words across decks. Cards with your own explanations, images, and recordings Anki Its official site documents media support, customizable card layouts, and add-ons. Choosing reading material around known vocabulary jpdb It connects vocabulary knowledge with its media database. Flashcards for several subjects, beyond Japanese Anki You can organize your own material into decks. Moving an existing collection A small trial first jpdb describes its Anki import as partial; migration should be checked before a full move. These are differences in workflow, not evidence that one produces faster learning for everyone. What jpdb is designed to do jpdb describes itself as a Japanese dictionary and learning system. Its homepage lists vocabulary extraction from text, prebuilt media decks, kanji study, and progress tracking across decks. jpdb’s public homepage links to media difficulty lists and describes text vocabulary extraction and prebuilt decks. Official website screenshot, October 22, 2026. Source . The connection between study and a specific piece of media is its main attraction. Rather than asking only which word to review next, you can ask which words stand between you and a novel you want to read. The site also describes helping users find material that overlaps with their known vocabulary. That can give review a visible purpose. A deck associated with something you care about may feel more meaningful than an unrelated list. Vocabulary overlap is still only part of difficulty. Knowing many words in a passage does not mean you will immediately understand its grammar, references, or implied meaning. Treat a vocabulary estimate as help choosing material, then read a sample yourself. What Anki is designed to do Anki is a flashcard program. Its official site documents synchronization through AnkiWeb, support for audio and images, customizable layouts and review timing, and add-ons. Anki’s official website lists synchronization, media support, customization, and add-ons. This is the public feature page, not an installed-app test. Official website screenshot, October 22, 2026. Source . For Japanese, that flexibility lets you decide what belongs on a card. You might keep a word with a sentence you understood, a short explanation of a confusing distinction, or audio from material you are permitted to use. You can also remove information that makes a card unnecessarily difficult. The tradeoff is that you make more decisions. Choosing a deck, editing cards, and adjusting a workflow all take attention. You do not need an elaborate setup to start, but customization can become a separate hobby if you let it. Use the official download page to identify the correct product for your device. It distinguishes the free desktop application, AnkiMobile for iOS, and the contributor-developed AnkiDroid for Android. Similar names in an app store do not establish that an app belongs to the same project. What learners like—and what they disagree about In a March 2024 Reddit discussion , the original poster said Anki reviews had become a chore. They found jpdb more motivating because a central vocabulary database connected their progress with anime and book decks. That is a useful account of motivation. It does not establish that jpdb's review system is objectively better. A reply from Scylithe described returning to Anki after using jpdb. Their concerns included customization, example material, and the time spent waiting between reviews. Other replies discussed backups and disagreed about export options. Those comments describe experiences from 2024. They should become questions to investigate in the current product, not a list of defects assumed to remain unchanged. There are also examples of people combining tools. In a July 2026 X post , a learner described using jpdb for vocabulary, WaniKani for kanji, Bunpro for grammar, and Japanese media for listening and reading. That is one person's routine, not a requirement to subscribe to several services. Before switching, identify the actual problem “I'm tired of Anki” can mean several things: The words have little connection to what you want to read. Too many new cards have created more review than you can comfortably finish. The prompts are ambiguous, or contain too much information. You spend more time maintaining cards than using Japanese. A different platform may help with some of these problems. Others can follow you into a new system. For example, a media deck may make your goal clearer, but adding more material than you can review will still consume time. Conversely, simplifying an Anki card may help if the problem is the card itself rather than the application. Describe the problem in one sentence. “I want less setup before studying a particular novel” is a better decision criterion than “I need the best SRS.” A small comparison you can make before migrating The following is an editorial suggestion, not a test we have completed. Choose one short text or a small group of words from material you want to understand. Try the relevant jpdb workflow and a simple Anki deck without changing your main collection. Compare the things you actually notice: how much setup you need, whether the example helps you understand the word, how easily you correct an unhelpful prompt, and how the process feels on your usual device. Then return to the original passage. Can you recognize the words there? A satisfying review session is useful, but the passage is why you started. A short trial can reveal friction and preferences. It cannot demonstrate long-term retention or predict which system you will still enjoy months later. Check migration and backup separately jpdb's homepage says it can partially import an existing Anki database . Do not read “partial” as a promise to preserve every card, field, media file, and scheduling detail. Before a substantial move, keep your original collection and confirm what the current import process accepts. The Anki export manual explains text exports and packaged decks, including options for media and scheduling information. Those formats serve different purposes, so choose the backup you intend rather than assuming every export preserves the same data. Check a small sample after importing. Also investigate how you would retrieve your data from the new system if you later wanted to leave. The older Reddit debate about exports does not settle the current answer. Verify it directly rather than relying on either the most reassuring or the most alarming reply. Leave room for reading and listening Whichever tool you choose, keep contact with the material that gives the vocabulary a purpose. Review can help you revisit words; reading and listening let you encounter how those words behave in context. If you want supported Japanese reading alongside flashcards, Satori Reader is another resource to investigate. If you are deciding how much structure you want around study, our renshuu review explores a different type of learning app. Add another tool when it solves a clear gap. A longer app list is not itself a better routine. Questions learners ask Is jpdb better than Anki for Japanese? It may suit you better if media decks and shared vocabulary progress reduce the work you dislike. Anki may suit you better if control over individual cards matters more. The sources here do not establish a universal winner. Can jpdb replace a complete Japanese course? Its vocabulary and kanji features serve particular study tasks. You will still need ways to understand grammar and use Japanese in meaningful contexts. Choose those around your current needs. Should I use both? You can, but first decide which job each will do. Duplicating the same daily reviews in two systems may create work without solving a new problem. What should I try first? If you already use one, start by fixing the specific part of your routine that feels difficult. If you are choosing from scratch, try one small workflow connected to Japanese you want to understand. Keep the option that makes it easier to return to that material. Sources jpdb official homepage : product features and partial Anki import, checked October 22, 2026. Anki official homepage and downloads : flashcard features and platform products, checked October 22, 2026. Anki export manual : export formats and included data, checked October 22, 2026. title: Language Transfer Spanish Too Fast? A Beginner Routine
text: Language Transfer Spanish Too Fast? A Slower Beginner Routine A slower way to approach Language Transfer: pause before answers, identify the step that confuses you, and leave room for Spanish beyond the explanations. October 22, 2026 Spanish If Language Transfer Spanish feels too fast, pause before the recorded student's answer and give yourself time to think. Work with a short section, identify one point you cannot follow, and return to it before moving on. You do not need to keep pace with the person in the recording for the activity to be useful. Start by separating three difficulties: understanding the English explanation, building the Spanish answer, and recognizing Spanish when you hear it. Each needs a slightly different response. The routine below is an editorial suggestion based on official course guidance and a linked learner discussion, checked on October 22, 2026. We have not tested it as a learning intervention or completed a lesson-by-lesson course assessment. Is Language Transfer suitable for beginners? The official Language Transfer FAQ says its courses are designed for beginners, while also explaining that they become advanced quickly. It describes the order and explanations as different from a conventional course. The official Complete Spanish page provides the lesson player and alternative ways to access the audio. No lesson playback or completion is claimed here. Official website screenshot, October 22, 2026. Source . That matters if you assume “beginner” means every activity will remain easy. You may understand an explanation when you hear it and still need more time to construct an answer independently. “Complete Spanish” is the course name, not a guarantee of complete command of Spanish. The FAQ describes the complete courses as exploring the language's structural landscape and developing a base for continued learning. It also encourages learners to use the language through reading, listening, and interaction after the course. You can find the official Complete Spanish course page , with links to the app, SoundCloud, YouTube, and audio downloads. The project describes its materials as free to access, without advertisements or required sign-ups. Donations support the project. One learner's experience of getting stuck In a May 2025 Reddit post , a complete beginner described enjoying the first lessons, then struggling to keep up. By lesson 14, even repeated listening left them feeling lost. That is one person's experience, not a finding that lesson 14 is universally too difficult. It does capture a recognizable problem: replaying a whole recording does not always reveal which step in an explanation you stopped following. Replies offered different approaches, including a slower audio course and more Spanish exposure alongside the explanations. They also disagreed about learning methods. You do not need to settle that entire debate to make your next session more manageable. First identify what you are trying to do when you get stuck. Find the point where you lose the thread What happens A useful next action You cannot follow the English explanation Pause and check the explanation, using the transcript if necessary. The explanation makes sense, but you cannot build the answer Leave more thinking time before hearing the model response. You copy the recorded answer without knowing how it was formed Go back to the question and work through the missing step. You answer in the lesson but struggle with other Spanish audio Add short, easier Spanish listening rather than only replaying explanations. Each new section feels harder and harder Reduce the amount you attempt and revisit the earlier point you need. These are practical distinctions, not diagnoses. You may experience more than one in the same session. Try to make the difficulty specific. “I forgot which form the question needs” gives you something to revisit. “I'm bad at languages” does not tell you what to do next. Pause before the answer, not only after it Hearing the answer can make it feel immediately familiar. That is different from reaching it on your own. When the instructor asks a question, pause before the recorded student answers. Think through your response without watching a transcript. If useful, try saying your answer, then listen to the response in the recording. If you disagree with the model, return to the relevant explanation. Was the difficulty meaning, a word you could not recall, or how the sentence was put together? Revisit that part rather than starting the entire lesson again automatically. There is no fixed response time you need to beat. A pause can make space for the thinking the activity asks of you. Use transcripts for support and revision A transcript can help you locate a passage or understand an English explanation. It can also make it easy to read an answer before you have tried to construct it. Language Transfer’s official FAQ explains when transcripts can support revision and warns that volunteer transcripts may contain mistakes. Official website screenshot, October 22, 2026. Source . The official FAQ advises against using transcripts during course time unless needed to follow the English. It particularly discourages looking at them while mentally constructing sentences. It does, however, describe using them for revision and finding specific parts of the course. The FAQ also warns that volunteer-created transcripts can contain mistakes. Treat unfamiliar spelling or a confusing line as something to verify, rather than automatically assuming that the transcript is correct. If you need a transcript to access the explanation, use it. Then, where possible, put it aside for the part where you try to form an answer yourself. Try this adjustable 15-minute session This is an example schedule, not an official Language Transfer timetable. The intervals are there to keep the session small; change them when an explanation needs more time. Time Activity First 2 minutes Return to one earlier question you remember and try answering without the model. Next 8 minutes Work through a short section, pausing before answers. You may cover only part of a track. Next 3 minutes Revisit one point that confused you, then attempt the question again. Last 2 minutes Stop playback and decide what you will return to next time. Do not force a whole track into the session just to finish it. If you spend the available time understanding one useful point, you have still done the work you selected. You can note a timestamp or question afterward if that helps you find it again. You do not need to transcribe the lesson while trying to follow it. Add Spanish you can actually follow A course can make a structure clearer without giving you enough experience recognizing it in different voices and situations. Leave some room for Spanish material outside the explanation. Choose a short item with a topic and difficulty you can follow. Dreaming Spanish is one video resource to investigate; Easy Spanish offers another route into conversations and interviews. Their formats and difficulty vary, so sample the material rather than assuming every video will suit a beginner. A modest task is enough: identify the topic, notice a familiar expression, or understand one short exchange. You do not have to extract every unknown word or turn the entire video into flashcards. If you understand almost nothing, find easier material. Struggling through a long, opaque recording is a different activity from listening to something you can partly understand. Should you repeat a lesson or move on? Repeat when you can name a question you want to answer differently. For example, you may want to understand why one response uses a particular structure or try it without hearing the model first. Move forward cautiously when you can follow the main reasoning, even if your response is slower than the recording. Keep the option to return. If the same missing step keeps disrupting later material, go back to that point. Replaying a long sequence without identifying the gap can turn review into an endurance exercise. You do not need a perfect record before continuing, but you should have some idea of what the next section builds on. When another resource may be a better next step If the pace and explanation style continue to frustrate you, it is reasonable to try another approach. That is a choice about fit, not a verdict on your ability. Pimsleur appeared in the Reddit discussion as a slower alternative preferred by some participants. That is a learner recommendation to investigate, not a timing comparison we have independently measured. Check a current sample before buying. You could also keep Language Transfer for occasional explanations while using a different beginner course as your main sequence. Choose one clear role for it, rather than making yourself complete it simply because other learners praise it. Questions beginners ask Can I learn Spanish from Language Transfer alone? Use it for what the course provides, then make room to hear, read, and use Spanish beyond the recordings. The official FAQ itself points learners toward broader exposure and interaction after the course. How many lessons should I do per day? Choose an amount that leaves time to think through the questions. For a difficult section, part of a lesson may be enough. There is no evidence here for a universal daily target. Should I write everything down? That is not necessary for the routine above. Follow the official advice about thinking without visual answers during the activity. Use a timestamp or brief reminder afterward if it helps you return to a specific point. What if I am slower than the recorded student? Pause. The recording can continue only when you let it. Your next useful step is to understand and attempt the question, not to match someone else's response time. Sources Language Transfer official homepage : access model and project information, checked October 22, 2026. Complete Spanish official course page : listening and download routes, checked October 22, 2026. title: Lingopie Japanese Review (2026): Worth It for Japanese Learners?
text: Lingopie Japanese Review 2026: Is It Good for Learning Japanese? Affiliate disclosure: This article contains affiliate links. If you sign up through my link, I may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Key Takeaways I tried Lingopie specifically for Japanese to see how useful that idea is in practice. This review covers the catalog, the learning tools, and whether the experience actually… September 22, 2026 Japanese Affiliate disclosure: This article contains affiliate links. If you sign up through my link, I may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Key Takeaways Lingopie has a Japanese catalog, but most content is beginner-level and platform-produced — not Japanese dramas or anime The core feature is clickable dual subtitles, but Japanese-specific challenges (no word spaces, verb conjugation) affect how well it works Most useful as a supplement for lower-intermediate learners; advanced learners will get more value from the Chrome extension on Netflix I tried Lingopie specifically for Japanese to see how useful that idea is in practice. This review covers the catalog, the learning tools, and whether the experience actually holds up for Japanese learners — including the parts that work differently for Japanese than they do for other languages. What Is Lingopie? Learn Japanese Online Free Lingopie is a language-learning platform built around TV shows, movies, short videos, and other native-language content. Instead of completing traditional textbook-style lessons, you watch content in the language you are learning and use built-in tools when you get stuck. The player includes clickable subtitles, translations, dual subtitles, flashcards, quizzes, playback controls, and vocabulary review tools. Words you click can be added to your word bank for later review. The basic learning loop looks like this: Watch → click unfamiliar words → understand them in context → save vocabulary → review later That immediately makes Lingopie feel different from apps built around isolated vocabulary drills. It sits somewhere between a streaming service and a language-learning app — and for Japanese specifically, that combination raises some interesting questions about how well it handles a language that works very differently from Spanish or French. Does Lingopie Have Japanese? Yes. Japanese is one of the languages you can learn on Lingopie. I selected it directly from the language menu in my account, and it appeared as my active language at the bottom of the interface. Lingopie has a Japanese-specific section of the catalog and promotes Japanese content including TV shows, movies, dramas, comedy, and beginner-friendly learning videos. The Japanese Catalog: What I Actually Found When I opened the Japanese catalog, the interface showed three filter dropdowns at the top — Effort , Duration , and Genres — and a level indicator in the top right corner showing Intermediate , with an option to change it. The left sidebar had four sections: Catalog , Short Stories (marked as new), Kids , and My Library . The main area was organized into rows. My Continue Watching row showed: Christmas Family — Japan, Easy Beyond Earth: Cosmic Wonders — Japan, Just right Daily News in Easy Japanese — Japan, Easy (labeled Powered by Lingopie) NihonGO Now! — Japan, Easy The Everybody’s Watching row below showed: Daily News in Easy Japanese — Easy Japanese 101 — Easy Myths and Fables of Japan for Kids — Easy Go Around the Trees — Easy Most of the homepage content is labeled Easy Almost every title on the homepage carried an Easy tag. The only exception in my Continue Watching row was Beyond Earth: Cosmic Wonders , which showed as Just right at Intermediate level. The Easy / Just right / Hard system adjusts relative to your set level, so the same content would display differently for a beginner versus an intermediate learner. This makes the difficulty labels more useful than a fixed scale. A significant portion of the catalog is Lingopie-produced Learn Japanese Online Free Daily News in Easy Japanese is explicitly labeled Powered by Lingopie , meaning Lingopie produces this content itself rather than licensing it from Japanese broadcasters. Japanese 101 and NihonGO Now! appear to be structured teaching shows hosted by presenters — created specifically for learners. This is worth knowing before you sign up. The Japanese catalog is not a collection of Japanese dramas or anime from Japanese broadcasting. A significant portion of what appears on the homepage is learning-focused content made for the platform. For beginners, this is actually an advantage. Daily News in Easy Japanese and NihonGO Now! are designed to be accessible from an early stage, with controlled vocabulary and clear speech. For intermediate or advanced learners who want to watch content that Japanese people actually watch, the catalog will feel more limited. The Kids section The sidebar includes a dedicated Kids section. For Japanese learners, this is worth taking seriously. Kids’ content in Japanese typically features slower speech, simpler sentence structures, high-frequency vocabulary, and strong visual context. Learners who would struggle with an adult drama can use the Kids section as a genuine entry point — the content is learner-appropriate regardless of your age. The Chrome extension for Netflix and Disney+ There is a promotion in the sidebar for a Chrome extension that brings Lingopie’s learning tools into Netflix and Disney+. For intermediate and advanced learners, this may be more valuable than the in-house catalog itself. It means you can use Lingopie’s clickable subtitles on a much larger library of actual Japanese content — dramas, anime, films — rather than being limited to Lingopie’s own beginner-focused videos. How Learning Japanese With Lingopie Works Dual subtitles and clickable words The player supports Japanese and English subtitles at the same time. Each word in the Japanese subtitle is clickable, giving you an instant translation and basic information about the word without pausing the video. This is the central feature of the platform. For most languages, it works straightforwardly. Japanese adds a layer of complexity: words are not separated by spaces, so the system has to identify word boundaries automatically before any clicking is possible. Lingopie handles this through tokenization — algorithmically splitting the continuous Japanese subtitle text into clickable units. For common vocabulary and standard sentence structures, this works reasonably well. For compound expressions or less common patterns, you may occasionally find that a click selects more or less than you intended. It is worth testing on a few different videos during the free trial to get a feel for how it behaves with the content you want to watch. Verb conjugation and dictionary lookup Japanese verbs change form constantly. You will encounter 食べました in a subtitle, but the dictionary form is 食べる. 行った becomes 行く. 見ている becomes 見る. 分からない becomes 分かる. Lingopie’s word lookup connects clicked words to translations. For straightforward vocabulary, this is useful. For conjugated verb forms, the quality of the lookup depends on how well the system recognizes the base form — and this varies. If you click a conjugated verb and get a clean dictionary entry with the base form and a clear meaning, the tool is doing its job. If it returns nothing useful or gives you a partial match, you will need to look it up separately. Furigana Furigana — the small hiragana characters above kanji that show pronunciation — is one of the most practically important features for Japanese learners below around N3 level. Without it, a subtitle containing unfamiliar kanji is difficult to even read aloud. Lingopie’s subtitles display Japanese text, and the click-to-translate feature covers meaning. Whether furigana appears on subtitles automatically or as a toggle option is something to check during your trial if reading support is a priority at your current level. Vocabulary saving and review Words you click can be saved to your word bank and reviewed later through flashcards and quizzes. This connects the watching experience directly to vocabulary study, which is one of the things that separates Lingopie from watching Japanese content on a regular streaming service. The review system is straightforward: saved words come back as flashcards, and Lingopie prompts you to review them over time. It is not as sophisticated as Anki’s spaced-repetition algorithm, but it is more integrated — the vocabulary is tied to the content where you heard it, which helps with memory in a way that isolated flashcard decks often do not. Playback controls Lingopie includes slow playback and sentence looping. Both are useful for Japanese specifically because natural speech speed is one of the first barriers learners run into with native content. Being able to slow a line down or loop it until you can hear the individual words clearly makes a noticeable difference to how much you actually absorb from each session. Why Japanese Is a Different Test Than Most Languages A feature can work smoothly for Spanish and still feel less useful for Japanese. Three challenges make Japanese worth examining separately: No spaces. Tokenization is not something most language-learning platforms have to think about for European languages. For Japanese, it is foundational to everything else. Verb conjugation. The gap between the form you see in a subtitle and the form in a dictionary is constant. A tool that handles conjugated forms well is significantly more useful than one that doesn’t. Kanji reading. Reading support matters at a stage where learners can follow vocabulary meaning but cannot yet read unfamiliar kanji aloud. Furigana bridges that gap in a way that a translation alone does not. These three factors are what determine whether Lingopie is genuinely better than alternatives for Japanese learners, rather than simply adequate. Is Lingopie Worth It for Japanese? Comparing It to Alternatives Lingopie vs. watching Japanese on Netflix directly Netflix has a much larger Japanese library — real dramas, anime, variety content, and films that Japanese audiences actually watch. Its limitation is the absence of any learning layer. You can add Japanese subtitles, but you cannot click words, save vocabulary, or loop individual sentences. Lingopie’s tools are designed to lower that friction. The Chrome extension is particularly relevant here: if it works reliably for Japanese Netflix content, it effectively gives you Lingopie’s learning layer on top of Netflix’s library — which is a compelling combination. Lingopie vs. Language Reactor Language Reactor is a free Chrome extension that adds dual subtitles and word lookup to Netflix and YouTube. For Japanese it includes furigana support. Its main advantage is that it costs nothing at the basic level. Lingopie’s advantage is the integrated catalog, the structured vocabulary review system, and a more complete platform experience. If you already have Netflix and primarily want clickable subtitles on Japanese content, Language Reactor is worth trying first. If you want a more structured system that combines content, word saving, and review in one place, Lingopie makes more sense. Lingopie vs. Anki Anki’s spaced-repetition algorithm is more sophisticated than Lingopie’s built-in flashcard system. Its limitation is that vocabulary often arrives disconnected from context — you are memorizing a definition without remembering where or why you encountered the word. Lingopie’s word saving creates cards tied directly to the show where you heard the word. For learners who find Anki abstract or hard to sustain, this context-driven approach is a meaningful advantage. Who Is Lingopie Actually Good For? Most useful for: Lower-intermediate learners (roughly N5 to N4) who want more listening practice with subtitle support Learners who find drilling boring and learn better from real content with context Intermediate learners who want to use the Chrome extension to study from Japanese Netflix content more actively Beginners already using a grammar resource who want to add listening practice alongside it Less useful for: Complete beginners with no Japanese grammar foundation yet — the content will feel overwhelming without some groundwork Advanced learners looking for a large library of authentic Japanese dramas or anime — the in-house catalog is not built for that audience Anyone whose primary goal is structured grammar instruction — Lingopie does not teach grammar systematically How I Would Use Lingopie for Japanese Rather than watching passively for an hour, I would use Lingopie in short, intentional sessions. First 5 minutes — watch without stopping. Play the content at normal speed without pausing for every unknown word. Try to follow the scene from Japanese, subtitles, tone, and context. Next 5 minutes — active replay. Go back to the same section. This time, click only words that seem genuinely useful to learn. Limit yourself to around five words per session — more than that and the review becomes unmanageable. Next 5 minutes — reduce English support. Turn off or cover the English subtitle and replay important lines. Listen for the words you just saved. Last 5 minutes — review and repeat aloud. Open the vocabulary deck and go through the words you just saved. Then go back to one or two sentences from the video and repeat the whole sentence aloud, not just the single word. Twenty minutes used this way will give you more than an hour of passive watching. Lingopie Pricing and Free Trial Lingopie offers monthly and annual subscription plans. The annual plan works out significantly cheaper per month than the monthly option. Lingopie currently offers a free trial for eligible sign-ups, which gives you access to the Japanese catalog and learning tools before committing to a paid plan. Lingopie’s documentation describes a 7-day trial, though availability can depend on the plan and how you sign up. I would use the trial to check three things specifically: Browse the full Japanese catalog beyond the homepage — filter by genre and scroll through to see whether there is content you actually want to watch at your level. Test the clickable subtitles on a few different videos to get a feel for how word selection works in Japanese. Try the Chrome extension on Netflix if you have Japanese content there — this may end up being the most useful part of the subscription for your level. Final Verdict Lingopie is a genuinely interesting platform for Japanese learners, but how useful it is depends heavily on where you are in your Japanese study. The catalog is weighted toward beginner and Easy content, with a mix of Lingopie-produced learning shows and licensed videos. For complete beginners and lower-intermediate learners, this is exactly what you want. For intermediate and advanced learners, the Chrome extension and its ability to work with Japanese Netflix content matters more than the in-house catalog. The learning tools — dual subtitles, word saving, vocabulary review — are the right idea for Japanese. Whether they handle Japanese’s specific challenges (word boundaries, verb conjugation, kanji reading) smoothly enough for your level is the honest question, and the free trial is the most direct way to find out. Lingopie is not a complete Japanese course. It does not teach grammar, provide structured kanji progression, or follow a JLPT syllabus. It is a supplement — one that could be genuinely valuable if you are at the stage where textbook Japanese feels too controlled but native Japanese still feels too fast.
