title: Lingopie vs Migaku (2026): Which Is Better for Japanese?
text: Lingopie vs Migaku for Japanese Learners (2026): Which One Is Actually Worth It? This post contains affiliate links. If you sign up through my links, I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you — and it helps keep this blog running. Thanks for your support! So you’ve been watching anime without subtitles and thinking, “I should really be learning something here.” Whether you’re a… September 22, 2026 Japanese This post contains affiliate links. If you sign up through my links, I may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you — and it helps keep this blog running. Thanks for your support! ⚡ 3 Things to Know Before You Read Lingopie is a streaming platform with its own Japanese content library — plug in and start watching immediately. Migaku is a toolkit that layers on top of Netflix and YouTube — more powerful, but requires setup. For most learners, Lingopie is the easier, more enjoyable way in — curated shows, zero setup, and built-in tools that make Japanese feel fun from day one. So you’ve been watching anime without subtitles and thinking, “I should really be learning something here.” Whether you’re a binge-watcher who wants to pick up Japanese naturally or a dedicated studier who wants to turn every episode into a vocabulary drilling session, you’ve probably landed on the Lingopie vs Migaku debate. Both promise to help you learn Japanese through content — but they work in completely different ways, and choosing the wrong one is an easy $100+ mistake to make. I spent time testing both tools with real Japanese content to give you an honest side-by-side comparison. Here’s everything you need to know. How I Tested These Tools Learn Japanese Online Free To keep this comparison fair, I ran both tools through the same scenario: a 20-minute Japanese anime clip on Netflix that I hadn’t seen before. I clicked the same set of words — including conjugated verbs like 食べました (ate), 行った (went), and 見ている (is watching) — and compared how each tool handled the lookup, what got saved to my flashcard deck, and how easy it was to actually review those cards afterward. I also spent time with Lingopie’s own content library, browsing its beginner and intermediate Japanese catalog and using its built-in quiz and playback features separately from the Netflix test. A few things I was specifically watching for: Does the tool correctly identify the base form of conjugated verbs? In Japanese this matters enormously — if your flashcard saves 食べました instead of 食べる, it’s basically useless. Is furigana (kana above kanji) available anywhere? For learners below N3, this is a non-trivial accessibility issue. How friction-free is the flashcard-to-review pipeline? A word lookup that never gets reviewed is just wasted attention. With that context in mind, here’s what I found. What Are Lingopie and Migaku? Before diving in, it helps to understand what each tool actually is . Lingopie is essentially a streaming platform built for language learners. Think of it as a Netflix-lite where all the shows come with built-in language learning features: dual subtitles, click-to-translate, flashcards, and quizzes. You pick a show, hit play, and the learning tools are baked right into the player. Learn Japanese Online Free Migaku is an immersion toolkit that attaches on top of platforms you already use — Netflix, YouTube, Disney+, and more. It’s a browser extension (plus mobile app) that adds instant word lookup, AI explanations, and one-click flashcard creation to any video content you’re watching. It also has its own SRS (spaced repetition system) called Migaku Memory, plus structured Japanese courses. The short version: Lingopie is a platform . Migaku is a tool layer you add to the content you already watch. Key Feature Comparison Feature Lingopie Migaku Content library ✅ Built-in (anime, dramas, podcasts, stories) ❌ Use your own (Netflix, YouTube, etc.) Dual subtitles ✅ Yes ✅ Yes (on supported platforms) Click-to-translate ✅ Yes ✅ Yes (with AI explanations) Furigana / kana hints ❌ No ✅ Yes (on lookup) Conjugation handling ❌ Weak ✅ Strong SRS flashcard system ✅ Built-in (basic) ✅ Full SRS (Migaku Memory) Anki export ❌ No ✅ Yes Beginner-level filters ✅ Yes ❌ Manual only Browser extension ❌ No ✅ Yes Mobile app ✅ Yes (iOS/Android/TV) ✅ Yes (iOS/Android) Structured courses ❌ Limited ✅ Yes (Kana, grammar, kanji) Playback speed control ✅ Yes (0.65× – 1×) ❌ Relies on platform Pricing ~$12/mo or ~$144/yr $10/mo, $96/yr, or $499 lifetime Free trial 7-day 10-day Content: Lingopie’s Biggest Advantage If you don’t have Netflix or aren’t sure where to find Japanese content, Lingopie wins here by default . It has its own curated library of Japanese TV shows, anime, dramas, comedies, podcasts, short stories, and even audiobooks — all tagged by difficulty level. You can filter by “Beginner,” “Intermediate,” or “Advanced” and start watching immediately without hunting for content elsewhere. Migaku has no content library of its own. You bring your own: your Netflix subscription, your YouTube watchlist, your Disney+ account. For a lot of learners this is actually a non-issue (you probably already have Netflix), but it’s worth knowing upfront — Migaku is a tool, not a service. Winner: Lingopie — especially for beginners who want a ready-to-go experience. Japanese Accuracy: Where Things Get Interesting This is where the two tools diverge significantly — and it matters a lot for Japanese specifically. Lingopie’s Japanese Parsing Issues Japanese is notoriously hard to parse because words don’t have spaces between them, and verbs conjugate heavily. During testing, Lingopie’s click-to-translate had a recurring problem: it would grab particles along with words . For example, clicking on ビールを飲みます (I drink beer) would sometimes save ビールを (beer + object marker を) as the flashcard word instead of just ビール (beer). This means your vocabulary list slowly fills with broken, particle-attached entries that are useless for actual study. On top of that, Lingopie shows no furigana — no kana hints above kanji characters. If you’re at a beginner or early intermediate level, this makes the subtitles harder to follow than they need to be. Translations are AI-generated and can be awkward or inaccurate. Migaku’s Lookup Quality Migaku uses actual Japanese dictionaries combined with AI (ChatGPT-style explanations), and it handles verb conjugations smartly. Clicking 食べました (the polite past tense of “to eat”) correctly identifies 食べる as the base form and saves the card accordingly. The popup shows: The dictionary form of the word Furigana (kanji readings) An example sentence with context An AI-generated explanation Audio pronunciation Cards created in Migaku are clean, linguistically accurate, and immediately useful. Winner: Migaku — by a significant margin for Japanese specifically. Flashcards and Review Systems Lingopie Flashcards Every word you click in Lingopie automatically gets added to your word list as a flashcard. The built-in review system includes multiple-choice vocabulary quizzes, a “Say It” speaking exercise, and a “Grammar Coach” feature that gives sentence-level explanations. It’s fun and approachable. The downside: Lingopie’s flashcards are stuck inside Lingopie . You can’t export them to Anki or any other SRS. If you ever stop subscribing, you lose access to everything you’ve studied. Migaku Memory (Full SRS) Migaku’s SRS system is much more robust. One click creates a card with sentence context, audio, AI explanation, furigana, and even pitch accent data. Cards sync across the web and mobile app, and you can export to Anki or CSV if you prefer to study there instead. If you’re someone who already uses Anki, Migaku slots right into your workflow. If you don’t, Migaku Memory works as a complete standalone system. Winner: Migaku — especially if you take vocabulary review seriously or use Anki. Ease of Use: Lingopie Keeps It Simple Here’s where Lingopie genuinely shines. The onboarding is seamless: sign up, pick a Japanese show, and start clicking words. There’s no extension to install, no setup process, no technical configuration. Everything is self-contained inside the Lingopie player. Migaku has more power, but that comes with more complexity. You need to install the Chrome extension, link it to your streaming platforms, and learn how the SRS system works. For learners who just want to watch anime and absorb some vocabulary without a steep learning curve, Migaku’s setup can feel like homework before the actual homework. Winner: Lingopie — for simplicity and plug-and-play experience. Who Each Tool Is Really For Choose Lingopie If… You’re a beginner or casual learner who wants to enjoy Japanese shows while picking up vocabulary naturally You want everything in one place — content, subtitles, flashcards, and quizzes — without managing multiple platforms You don’t have Netflix or don’t want to hunt for Japanese content yourself You learn best through fun, low-pressure exposure rather than structured drilling You want slow playback options (Lingopie lets you watch at 0.65× speed, which is huge for beginners) Choose Migaku If… You’re serious about building Japanese vocabulary and want a reliable, accurate SRS pipeline You already watch anime or dramas on Netflix or YouTube and want to mine vocabulary from what you’re already watching You use or want to use Anki , and want your flashcards to integrate with it You’re targeting JLPT and want more systematic vocabulary and grammar coverage You don’t mind a learning curve in exchange for a more powerful tool Lingopie vs Migaku by Learning Level Generic “beginner vs advanced” breakdowns can feel vague, so here’s a more specific take based on where most Japanese learners actually find themselves. Absolute Beginners (Just Starting Out) If you don’t know hiragana yet, neither tool is a magic shortcut — you’ll need to learn the kana first, full stop. That said, Migaku has a structured beginner course that walks you through hiragana, katakana, and foundational grammar before you ever touch a video. Think of it as onboarding for immersion. Lingopie doesn’t offer a kana course. It assumes you’ll learn to read through exposure, which works in some cases but can be frustrating when you’re clicking words you literally cannot read. What Lingopie does offer is slow playback (down to 0.65× speed) and beginner-filtered show selections, which remove the overwhelm of picking content yourself. At this level: Start with Migaku’s beginner courses to build your kana and basic grammar foundation, then switch to Lingopie’s curated beginner shows for low-stakes listening practice once you can read hiragana. Early Intermediate (Around N4–N3) This is the level where immersion starts to click. You know enough grammar to follow simple sentences, and your listening is getting faster. Both tools become genuinely useful here. Lingopie’s intermediate-tagged shows give you content that’s challenging but not discouraging. The click-to-translate function works well enough for common nouns and adjectives. The parsing problems are most noticeable with verbs — so if you’re mining vocabulary, stick to clicking nouns and set phrases rather than verb conjugations. Migaku shines at this level because early intermediate learners typically encounter a huge number of unknown words per episode. Migaku’s one-click card creation with full sentence context means you can capture 10–15 new words per episode and actually review them later. The SRS ensures that words spiral back to you before you forget them. At this level: Migaku is the better vocabulary-building investment. Use Lingopie for comfort watching — shows you want to enjoy without pressure. Upper Intermediate to Advanced (N2 and Above) At this point, you’re watching shows for enjoyment as much as study, and unknown words are a smaller percentage of each episode. This is where Lingopie becomes surprisingly pleasant — the learning friction is low, the content variety is solid, and the experience genuinely feels like watching TV rather than studying. Migaku is still powerful for mining specific vocabulary (technical words, unusual expressions, regional dialect), but the pressure to review 50 cards a day starts to outweigh the fun for many learners at this level. The pitch accent trainer and grammar coach are still useful for fine-tuning. At this level: Lingopie for daily immersion enjoyment; Migaku selectively when you want to go deep on new vocabulary domains. JLPT-Focused Learners If you’re actively studying for JLPT N3, N2, or N1, Migaku is the clearer choice . The structured SRS, Anki compatibility, and grammar breakdowns align much better with the kind of deliberate study that JLPT prep requires. You can mine vocabulary from content and feed it directly into a level-appropriate Anki deck. Lingopie’s quiz system isn’t calibrated to JLPT vocabulary lists, and there’s no way to target specific grammar patterns. It can supplement your study as a listening tool, but it won’t replace a proper exam prep system. Can You Use Both Lingopie and Migaku Together? The short answer is yes — and for a certain type of learner, this is actually the ideal setup. Here’s one way to think about it: Lingopie is your passive input time. Migaku is your active study time. When you’re tired after work and just want to watch something in Japanese without thinking too hard, Lingopie is there with a pre-selected show at the right difficulty level. The dual subtitles keep you anchored, and clicking the occasional word keeps you semi-engaged. It’s the Japanese learning equivalent of reading a book in your target language on the couch. When you sit down specifically to build vocabulary — maybe 20–30 focused minutes on a Saturday morning — you open Netflix with Migaku running. You watch more intentionally, pause to look up new words, create cards for anything useful, and then spend 10 minutes reviewing in Migaku Memory. The two tools aren’t in competition. They serve different moments in a learning week. The only real caveat: Lingopie flashcards can’t be exported , so whatever vocabulary you save there lives only in Lingopie. If you’re serious about long-term vocabulary retention, Migaku (with its Anki export) is a more portable investment. Pricing Breakdown Plan Lingopie Migaku Monthly ~$12/mo ~$10/mo Annual ~$144/yr (often discounted to ~$72) $96/yr Lifetime Occasionally available $499 Free Trial 7 days 10 days Refund policy Cancel anytime 14-day money-back guarantee At face value, the pricing is similar. But Migaku’s $499 lifetime deal is worth considering if you’re in it for the long haul — it covers all languages, not just Japanese, so if you ever pick up Korean, Chinese, or Spanish, you’re covered. One note on free trials: both require a payment method upfront. Lingopie users have reported difficulty canceling before the trial ends, so set a reminder. The Verdict Lingopie Migaku 🎯 Best for 🎬 Casual learners, beginners, binge-watchers 📚 Serious learners, JLPT studiers, SRS users 🈶 Japanese accuracy ⚠️ Weak (particle issues, no furigana) ✅ Strong (dictionary + AI, conjugation-aware) 📺 Content access 🗂️ Built-in curated library 🔗 Your own Netflix/YouTube 🃏 Review system 🎮 Basic quizzes 🧠 Full SRS with Anki export 🖱️ Ease of use 😌 Very easy 🔧 Moderate setup required 💰 Value for money 🛋️ Good for casual use 💪 Better for active vocabulary building If your goal is to actually retain Japanese vocabulary and build fluency through immersion , Migaku is the stronger tool. Its pipeline — watch content, click unknown words, review with SRS — is well-designed, linguistically accurate, and built to scale with your level. That said, Lingopie is genuinely enjoyable . If you’re an intermediate or advanced learner who just wants to consume Japanese content with a helpful safety net of translations and instant lookups, Lingopie makes that experience smooth and fun. It’s also a solid choice if you’re a complete beginner who wants access to leveled content without worrying about finding the right shows. The best setup? Use both: Lingopie for curated, guided content time — especially when you want to relax and let Japanese wash over you — and Migaku when you’re in “study mode” and want every unfamiliar word to end up in a flashcard. → Read our full Lingopie Japanese review Lingopie vs Migaku Frequently Asked Questions Does Lingopie have a good Japanese anime selection? Yes — Lingopie specifically markets its Japanese anime and J-drama catalog under categories like “Best of Japan” and “Best Cartoons.” The library isn’t as large as Netflix’s, but it’s curated for learners, which means you won’t accidentally click on something way above your level. Can Migaku work with anime on YouTube? Yes. Migaku works with YouTube as well as Netflix, Disney+, and Rakuten Viki. Most classic anime and many new releases have official YouTube channels with full episodes, so you can often find what you’re looking for without a Netflix subscription. Do either of these tools show furigana on subtitles? Lingopie does not show furigana anywhere — not on subtitles, not on flashcards. Migaku shows kanji readings when you look up a word through its popup, and exported Anki cards often include furigana as well. Neither tool overlays furigana on the running subtitles in real time. Can I use Migaku on my phone? Yes. Migaku has iOS and Android apps that support YouTube content and manually imported videos. However, some features — particularly Netflix integration — are Chrome extension only, meaning you’ll need a desktop browser for that. Lingopie has full iOS/Android apps and even smart TV support (FireTV, Roku). Is Lingopie or Migaku better for Korean learners too? Both tools support multiple languages beyond Japanese. Lingopie has a Korean content library with K-dramas and variety shows. Migaku supports Korean through its extension and courses. If you’re studying both Japanese and Korean (or thinking about it), Migaku’s single subscription covers all its supported languages — which arguably gives it better long-term value. What happens to my Lingopie flashcards if I cancel? You lose access. Lingopie’s vocabulary lists and flashcard data are tied to your account and subscription. There’s no export function, so if you cancel, everything you’ve saved disappears. This is one of the more significant reasons to think twice about using Lingopie as your primary vocabulary tool for serious study — Migaku’s export options mean your work travels with you. Is there a permanent free version of either tool? Neither offers a free tier. Both require a paid subscription after the trial period (7 days for Lingopie, 10 days for Migaku). Migaku’s 14-day money-back guarantee is more generous as a safety net if you decide it’s not for you after the trial. Have you tried either Lingopie or Migaku for Japanese? Drop a comment below and let me know which one worked better for you — or if there’s another tool I should test next. title: Renshuu Review (2026): Is It Worth Using for Japanese?
text: Renshuu Review (2026): I Expected a Flashcard App. I Got a Japanese Learning Toolbox. Affiliate disclosure: This post contains affiliate links to some tools mentioned (such as LingQ and ElevenLabs). I may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Renshuu did not sponsor this review and I was not compensated by them in any way. All opinions are my own. I started this Renshuu review expecting another… August 24, 2026 Japanese Affiliate disclosure: This post contains affiliate links to some tools mentioned (such as LingQ and ElevenLabs). I may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Renshuu did not sponsor this review and I was not compensated by them in any way. All opinions are my own. I started this Renshuu review expecting another Japanese SRS app with vocabulary, kanji, and grammar. Then I opened the Grammar Library. Then the kanji dictionary. Then the Text Analyzer. Then I realized I could tap words inside example sentences, listen to natural-sounding audio, browse community usage notes, study by JLPT level, and analyze my own Japanese text. Renshuu feels less like one Japanese course and more like a Japanese learning toolbox. And a surprising amount of it is free. Quick Summary My experience Best for Beginner to intermediate learners who like controlling what they study Levels Beginner through advanced / JLPT N5–N1 Main areas Vocabulary, grammar, kanji, sentences, kana, JLPT study Audio Lots of natural-sounding example audio Grammar One of Renshuu’s strongest areas Kanji Detailed and highly interconnected JLPT Very useful for structured review Free version Surprisingly generous Biggest downside So many features that it can feel overwhelming My verdict One of the most useful free Japanese study tools I have tried What Is Renshuu? Renshuu is a Japanese learning platform that combines vocabulary, kanji, grammar, sentences, kana study, JLPT content, review schedules, dictionaries, community notes, and other study tools in one place. What makes it different from a simple flashcard app is how connected everything feels. A kanji can lead to vocabulary. A vocabulary item can lead to example sentences and audio. A sentence can contain a word you can tap to see its reading, conjugation, dictionary form, and meaning. A grammar point can lead to more examples, usage notes, and related structures. That connected structure is the main reason I kept exploring. Renshuu Vocabulary: Small Reviews, Lots of Examples Vocabulary lessons are broken into small groups. In the schedule I tested, I learned around six new items, reviewed them, and then moved on to the next group. I liked that pacing. It felt much less tiring than opening a long flashcard queue and seeing dozens of unfamiliar words at once. More importantly, Renshuu rarely leaves a word isolated. You do not just see: 雨 = rain A word can lead to pronunciation, meanings, example sentences, and additional usage. When I opened 雨 , I could expand a large collection of examples such as: 曇 り 時々 雨 でした。 It was cloudy with occasional rain. 今年 は 雨 がほとんど 降 らない。 It rains very little this year. 朝 から 雨 が 降 っている。 It has been raining since the morning. 雨 から 雪 に 変 わった。 The rain changed into snow. 3日 続 けて 雨 が 降 った。 It rained for three days in a row. The target word is highlighted clearly, furigana is easy to see, and many examples include audio. That makes it easier to learn 雨が降る as a real combination instead of memorizing separate dictionary entries. Renshuu gives you plenty of examples and review options, but a repeatable routine still matters. My guide on how to learn Japanese vocabulary covers practical ways to remember words instead of repeatedly relearning them. The audio was one of my biggest surprises A lot of the example audio sounds remarkably natural. I also noticed that recordings often sounded like different speakers rather than one identical synthetic voice repeating every sentence. That variety made listening much more interesting. I would not claim that every recording on Renshuu is human-recorded without knowing the source of every audio file, but the overall experience sounds much more natural than I expected from a free Japanese study tool. Renshuu lists over 45,000 native-speaker recordings across its vocabulary and sentence database. For a free platform, that is an impressive number. Renshuu Grammar Library: What Makes It Stand Out The Grammar Library is probably my favorite part of Renshuu. You can browse grammar by JLPT level and by function. For example, grammar can be grouped into areas such as: Time Secondary Verbs Verb Suffixes Change & Cause/Effect Sentence Links Commands / Requests I find this much more useful than looking at one giant N3 grammar list. It lets me compare expressions that perform similar functions. A grammar entry can include: the Japanese structure a short English explanation JLPT level textbook references example sentences furigana English translations audio mastery tracking discussion and usage notes The color coding is genuinely useful Renshuu uses color very well. Target grammar is often highlighted in green. Variables such as A and B use different colors. Audio, community notes, and mastery information are visually separated. That matters because some pages are information-dense. The interface can look busy, but the color system usually makes the important part easy to find. English explanations work especially well for me Renshuu is primarily English-based. For some learners, that may be a limitation. For me, it is actually an advantage. With grammar in particular, seeing a Japanese structure beside a familiar English function often helps me understand the logic faster than memorizing a translated definition. For example, a structure might be explained as: Before A happens, B or: The first B since A occurred That gives me a framework for understanding what the Japanese grammar is doing. I find that easier to remember than learning one short translation with no sense of how the structure works. You can tap unfamiliar words without leaving the lesson This is a small feature that became one of my favorites. When I do not know a word inside an example sentence, I can tap it. Renshuu can show information such as: reading current conjugated form dictionary form English definitions pronunciation For example, tapping 忘れない can lead back to 忘れる while also showing that the form in the sentence is a casual present negative. That means I do not have to stop studying, open another dictionary, search the word, work out the conjugation, and then return. The learning flow stays intact. This is one of the best examples of how interconnected Renshuu feels: grammar → example → unknown word → conjugation → dictionary → audio Renshuu Kanji and Kana Tools Renshuu’s kanji section is another area where I kept discovering more features. You can open a character and immediately see vocabulary that uses it. For 文 , for example, the dictionary can lead to: 注文（ちゅうもん） 文句（もんく） 文句を言う（もんくをいう） Each word can then lead to readings, meanings, example sentences, and audio. So instead of memorizing: 文 = writing / sentence you start seeing: kanji → different readings → real words → example sentences → audio That becomes much more useful once you move beyond beginner Japanese. Kanji component explanations make memorization more interesting Renshuu also tries to explain kanji through their components. Instead of only asking you to memorize: character → reading → meaning it gives you additional visual or component-based ways to remember the character. Not every mnemonic should be treated as historical kanji etymology, but as a memory tool I found it much more interesting than repeatedly flipping the same character card. Kana study has more depth than I expected The kana charts include: hiragana and katakana pronunciation romaji stroke order writing diagrams mnemonics The mnemonic section is community-driven. Users can submit their own ways of remembering a character, and you can see which ones other learners liked. Some are useful. Some are strange. Some are memorable precisely because they are strange. Some pronunciation controls are easy to miss One interesting UX detail is that not every pronunciation feature has an obvious speaker icon. For example, combinations such as: しゃ しゅ しょ can be tapped directly to hear the pronunciation. That is useful once you discover it. But Renshuu sometimes hides interactive features a little too well. Is Renshuu Good for JLPT Study? Yes, especially for learners who like structured review without following one rigid course. You can browse grammar from N5 through N1 . But Renshuu does not stop at sorting everything by test level. Grammar is also grouped by function. That makes it easier to review related ideas together instead of memorizing hundreds of isolated patterns. You can move between areas involving: time cause and effect sentence linking commands requests negation degree expectations necessity This is one of the parts I think JLPT learners will appreciate most. Many grammar lessons include video explanations Some grammar lessons have a small video icon beside them. Those lessons include additional video-style explanations. I saw video lessons attached to topics such as: giving and receiving passive voice causative verbs honorific speech sentence links conjunctions commands and requests Not every grammar lesson has one. But there are more video lessons than I expected. The guided lessons were not my favorite The guided grammar lessons were probably my least favorite part of Renshuu. They are clear. They use large text, furigana, examples, and English explanations. But the slide-by-slide format felt passive to me. I found myself pressing Next through something that felt a little like a PowerPoint presentation. I was much more engaged when I could explore the Grammar Library, listen to examples, open related words, and compare structures myself. I learn much better when grammar is connected to something I can actually hear. I use structured study alongside real Japanese audio, and my guide to Japanese podcasts has options for different levels and listening styles. For me, Renshuu is at its best when it feels like an interactive Japanese reference system rather than a linear course. Renshuu Text Analyzer: Study Your Own Japanese The Text Analyzer was one of the features that surprised me most. You can paste your own Japanese text into Renshuu. I tested it with a short Japanese news passage. Renshuu analyzed: total words unique words how many words it thought I knew JLPT distribution of vocabulary number of kanji how many kanji I knew how much of the text I could read grammar expressions JLPT distribution of grammar It also added furigana to the passage. This makes the analyzer useful for answering a very practical question: Is this Japanese text actually appropriate for my level? You could use it with: an NHK article a podcast transcript a YouTube transcript a short story song lyrics reading practice LingQ takes the real-content approach further by turning articles, transcripts, podcasts, and other input into a reading-and-listening study system. Learn Japanese Online Free Renshuu feels stronger to me when I want structured grammar, kanji, JLPT study, and review in the same place. What is free and what needs Pro? During my testing, the analysis itself was available for free. I could paste text and see its vocabulary, kanji, grammar, JLPT distribution, and readability information. Turning those results directly into a new Renshuu list or study schedule was marked as a Pro feature. The free version also caps Text Analyzer input at 25,000 characters. Pro raises that to 500,000 — enough for very long texts or multiple chapters of reading material. That feels like a reasonable dividing line. Using transcripts for real Japanese study Podcast transcripts work especially well with this kind of workflow. I listen to YUYUの日本語Podcast for longer-form Japanese, and transcript-based material gives me something I can inspect before listening again. I can check unfamiliar vocabulary, notice grammar I missed the first time, and then return to the audio with much more context. One extra way I would use it for listening practice A useful Japanese passage does not always come with audio. ElevenLabs is useful for turning short Japanese passages into audio for repeated listening or shadowing. Listen Japanese Online Free I can paste a short passage, generate audio, and listen several times before practicing aloud. Renshuu already contains a lot of audio, so I would mainly use ElevenLabs for Japanese content I bring in myself. That gives me a simple workflow: find useful Japanese → analyze it → listen → repeat If you want to make the most of that final listening step, my guide on shadowing for language learning covers how the technique works and why it builds fluency faster than passive listening alone. Renshuu Community Notes: Textbook Japanese vs Real Japanese Another feature I did not expect was the community layer. Grammar entries and example sentences can contain Discussion & Notes . Some notes explain details that textbooks often skip. For example, a usage note for ている explained the conversational contraction: ている → てる ています → てます with examples showing how the shorter forms appear in natural speech. There are also community-created kana mnemonics and other comments throughout the site. I would still treat user notes as supplementary material rather than unquestionable grammar rules. But they often add useful context. This is especially helpful when you want to understand the difference between textbook Japanese and the way something may sound in conversation. Renshuu Free vs Pro: Is the Free Version Enough? The free version was much more capable than I expected. I could already use a large part of the: vocabulary system kanji tools Grammar Library sentence database JLPT resources kana tools community notes Text Analyzer without paying. I did encounter several Pro features. For example, some schedule settings marked sentence questions as Pro. The Text Analyzer also required Pro when I wanted to turn a passage directly into a new list or schedule. Pro pricing (as of August 2026): Monthly — $6.99/month (first month $3.49) Annual — $49.99/year Lifetime — $109.99 one-time payment Renshuu also donates 5% of all Pro sales to charity. Check the Renshuu pricing page to confirm current rates before purchasing. But I never felt that the free version existed only to push me toward a subscription. There was already enough available to build a serious Japanese study routine. I would start with free. Then I would consider Pro after I knew which advanced features I actually wanted. How Renshuu Compares to Anki and WaniKani If you are choosing between Renshuu and other popular Japanese tools, here is a quick comparison: Renshuu Anki WaniKani Free access Generous free version Free on desktop and Android; iOS app is paid Levels 1–3 free; subscription after Grammar Excellent built-in library Entirely deck-dependent Very limited Kanji Detailed, connected to vocabulary Deck-dependent Core focus Audio Extensive native examples Deck-dependent Some JLPT coverage Strong N5–N1 Deck-dependent Partial Setup required Minimal High Minimal Best for All tools in one place DIY flashcard system Kanji-focused learners Anki is flexible but requires you to find or build your own decks and configure everything from scratch. WaniKani takes a very focused approach to kanji and vocabulary but offers almost nothing for grammar. Renshuu sits between them: more structure than Anki, more freedom than WaniKani, and stronger grammar coverage than either. What I Like About Renshuu Three things stand out most. The Grammar Library is genuinely excellent. Being able to browse by function rather than just by JLPT level makes it far easier to compare similar structures and understand when to use one over another. I have not seen this done as well in any other free Japanese tool. The audio surprised me more than anything else. For a free platform, the amount of example audio is impressive, and many recordings sound natural rather than robotic. Having different-sounding voices across examples makes listening far less monotonous. The interconnected design is what keeps me coming back. Clicking a word in a grammar example leads somewhere useful. Opening a kanji leads to real vocabulary. Nothing feels isolated. Beyond those three: ✓ Extremely customizable study schedules ✓ Strong JLPT N5–N1 organization ✓ Lots of example sentences ✓ Tap words to see readings, conjugations, and dictionary forms ✓ Deep kanji dictionary ✓ Kana audio, stroke order, and mnemonics ✓ Useful Text Analyzer for your own Japanese ✓ Community usage notes add extra nuance ✓ A surprisingly generous free version What I Don’t Like About Renshuu The number of features can be overwhelming at first Renshuu has menus inside menus inside more menus. I repeatedly discovered useful features that I had no idea existed. Some clickable features are not obvious I only discovered some pronunciation controls because I happened to click the text. I did not enjoy every learning format equally The slide-style guided lessons felt much less engaging to me than the Grammar Library, audio examples, and interactive dictionary tools. None of these were deal-breakers. They are mostly the trade-off for having an enormous amount of functionality in one place. Who Is Renshuu Best For? I would especially recommend Renshuu to learners who: already know what they want to study are preparing for the JLPT like learning grammar through examples want vocabulary, kanji, and grammar connected together prefer customizing their own study routine want a strong free Japanese learning tool enjoy exploring resources instead of following one rigid course It may be less appealing when what you want is an app that simply tells you: Do lesson 1 → do lesson 2 → do lesson 3 Renshuu gives you much more freedom than that. That freedom is one of its greatest strengths. It also means you need to decide how you want to use it. Renshuu Review FAQs Is Renshuu completely free? Renshuu has a generous free version that covers vocabulary, kanji, grammar, JLPT resources, audio, the Text Analyzer, and community notes. Certain features — including some advanced schedule settings and turning Text Analyzer results directly into study lists — require a Pro subscription. Is Renshuu good for beginners? Yes, especially if you are comfortable learning at your own pace. Renshuu covers kana, N5 vocabulary, and beginner grammar clearly. That said, complete beginners who want a highly guided experience may find apps like Duolingo easier to start with before moving to Renshuu once they have the basics. How does Renshuu compare to Anki? Anki is a general flashcard app that requires you to find or build your own Japanese decks. Renshuu comes with vocabulary, kanji, grammar, audio, and JLPT resources built in and ready to use. For Japanese study specifically, Renshuu requires far less setup and gives you far more reference material out of the box. Is Renshuu good for JLPT preparation? Yes. JLPT N5–N1 vocabulary and grammar are well organized and browsable. Renshuu also groups grammar by function rather than just by test level, which makes it much easier to compare and remember similar structures during review. Can I use Renshuu on mobile? Yes. Renshuu has dedicated apps for both Android (Google Play) and iOS (App Store), in addition to the web version. Final Thoughts: Is Renshuu Worth It? Yes. Renshuu is one of the rare Japanese learning tools where I kept finding useful features the longer I explored it. My favorite part is not one specific flashcard system or game. It is how everything connects. Kanji → vocabulary → example sentences → audio Grammar → examples → unknown words → conjugations Real Japanese text → analysis → vocabulary and grammar That makes Renshuu feel more like a Japanese learning environment than a single-purpose app. I would personally spend most of my time in the Grammar Library, vocabulary examples, kanji tools, and Text Analyzer , rather than following every guided lesson from beginning to end. Considering how much of that I could use for free, Renshuu is very easy for me to recommend. Overall rating: 4.7 / 5 Category Score Grammar tools 5.0 / 5 Free version value 5.0 / 5 Vocabulary system 4.5 / 5 Audio quality 4.5 / 5 Kanji tools 4.5 / 5 Ease of use 3.5 / 5 → Try Renshuu for free More to explore Browse all Japanese jpdb vs Anki for Japanese: Media Decks or Custom Flashcards? title: Shadowing for Language Learning: 5 Steps to Real Speaking
text: How to Do Shadowing for Language Learning: 5 Steps That Turn Imitation Into Real Speaking I used shadowing for language learning for weeks and thought I was making great progress. I could keep up with a podcast, match the rhythm, and almost sound like the speaker while the clip was playing. Then I turned it off — and suddenly I could not say the same things on my own. That… August 16, 2026 Learn Better I used shadowing for language learning for weeks and thought I was making great progress. I could keep up with a podcast, match the rhythm, and almost sound like the speaker while the clip was playing. Then I turned it off — and suddenly I could not say the same things on my own. That was the problem I kept running into. I was getting better at copying the speaker, but not necessarily better at speaking by myself. Shadowing is genuinely useful for pronunciation, rhythm, and listening. But imitation and independent speaking are not quite the same skill. When you shadow, the speaker is giving you the words and rhythm in real time. When you speak on your own, you have to find the words yourself. In this guide, I will show you the shadowing routine I use to bridge that gap, so what you practise with audio becomes something you can actually use in conversation. Quick Start: Try This With One 45-Second Clip You do not need to read the whole guide first. Here is what to do right now with any short clip. 1. Listen once. No transcript. Catch the general meaning. 2. Check the transcript. Look up only what you missed. 3. Shadow two to three times with the transcript. Notice rhythm, stress, and how words connect. 4. Hide the transcript and shadow two to three times. Do not chase perfect synchronisation. 5. Record yourself once. Find the one most noticeable gap between your voice and the original. 6. Turn everything off and speak for 30 seconds. Use one or two expressions from the clip for something you would actually say yourself. The sections below explain why each step is built this way — and what to do when any of them feels stuck. Key Takeaways Shadowing works best with short, comprehensible audio from a speaker you actually want to sound like. Do not begin by copying sounds you do not understand. Comprehension comes before imitation. Record yourself and compare — do not rely on how you sound in your own head. Always finish with independent speaking so the language does not stay permanently tied to the original audio. What Is Shadowing in Language Learning? Shadowing means repeating what you hear almost immediately after hearing it — not waiting for a full sentence to finish, but following the speaker with a slight delay of half a second to one second. It is worth separating three techniques that often get confused: Technique How it works Best for Listen and repeat Hear a full sentence, wait for it to end, then repeat Memorising phrases at your own pace Shadowing Speak almost simultaneously with a 0.5–1 second delay Rhythm, intonation, and real-time response Delayed repetition Hear a longer passage, pause, then reproduce what you remember Memory and recall practice All three are useful. Shadowing specifically trains your ear and mouth to respond quickly to real-time speech. It is particularly good at building pronunciation habits and listening speed. What Shadowing Is Actually Good For When done consistently with appropriate material, shadowing can improve: Pronunciation — individual sounds and how they connect in real speech Rhythm and stress — where sentences naturally rise, fall, and pause Intonation — the patterns that carry emotion and meaning Connected speech — how words blur and link together at natural speed Listening speed — your ability to process audio without falling behind Pattern recognition — hearing familiar structures automatically, without translating These are real improvements. Shadowing is not hype. But there is one thing it does not automatically teach you: how to build your own sentence. Shadowing develops your ability to reproduce language. Producing language independently is a different skill, and most shadowing routines never address it. That gap is what this guide is designed to close. Why Shadowing Sometimes Does Not Improve Your Speaking Before getting into the method, it is worth understanding what goes wrong — because most people make the same mistakes. You Are Copying Sounds You Do Not Understand If you shadow material you cannot understand, you are doing phonetic mimicry, not language learning. You might still get some pronunciation practice, but the language is much harder to retain because there is little meaning to attach it to. Meaning should come before imitation. The Material Is Too Difficult Fast audio is not automatically better. If large parts of the clip are unclear, you are mostly chasing sounds. When the input is overwhelming, it becomes much harder to process meaning and produce output at the same time. Difficulty should be a slight stretch, not a sprint. You Never Listen to Yourself Most people shadow and trust that they sound good because the experience feels smooth. It often sounds different on playback. Recording yourself and listening back can feel uncomfortable, but it gives you a much more honest reference than judging your pronunciation while you are speaking. You Stop at Imitation This is the biggest issue. If every session ends with the audio still playing, you never practise speaking without a model. You train yourself to be dependent on the original speaker. When the audio disappears, so does your ability to produce the language. The five-step method below addresses all of this. How to Do Shadowing for Language Learning in 5 Steps Step 1. Choose a 30–60 Second Clip You Can Mostly Understand Start with a short clip you mostly understand and a speaker you actually want to sound like. Length matters. Most people pick something too long. A single minute of dense audio contains more than enough material for one productive session. Good sources include podcasts, YouTube videos, drama dialogue, interviews, and news clips. The format matters less than the content. Three criteria for choosing material: Interesting. If you are bored by the content, your attention will drift and retention will drop. Understandable. You should be able to follow the meaning with a little effort. Unknown words are fine. Unknown everything is not. Worth sounding like. Not every native speaker is a useful model. Regional accents, very fast informal speech, or heavy use of filler sounds may not be what you want to internalise at this stage. Because you are deliberately imitating the speaker, choose a voice and speaking style you would actually like to approximate. Step 2. Listen for Meaning Before You Shadow Listen first, check the transcript second, then start shadowing. Do not shadow on the first listen. Play the clip once and focus only on comprehension. Notice: What is the speaker saying overall? Which sentences did you miss completely? Which words did you recognise in context but would not have caught at speed? If you have a transcript, follow this order: listen first, then read . Looking at the text while listening tends to shift attention to the written form rather than the sound. This step is not optional. If you skip it, you shadow without meaning — which is exactly the problem described in the previous section. Move on when: you understand the main idea and can describe the clip in one sentence. Step 3. Shadow With the Transcript Now shadow, with the transcript in front of you. Your goal here is not speed. You are listening for: Pauses — where does the speaker naturally breathe or break? Stress — which words carry the weight of the sentence? Rhythm — what is the overall beat and flow? Reductions — where do sounds disappear or blend together? Sentence endings — how does intonation fall or rise at the end? As a concrete example, take a sentence like: “I didn’t even realise how much time had passed.” Said naturally, it might sound closer to: “I didn’t eeven realise how much time’d passed.” The written form and the spoken form are different. Shadowing with the transcript helps you map one onto the other. Do not worry about matching the speaker perfectly. Focus on noticing the patterns. Move on when: you can follow most of the sentence without constantly stopping to catch up. Step 4. Shadow Without the Transcript Close the transcript and shadow the same clip again. Start with a delay of half a second to one second behind the speaker. As you become more comfortable, you can close the gap — but do not make speed the goal. You do not need perfect synchronisation. Shadowing is not a performance. Falling slightly behind is fine. Losing a word and picking back up is fine. The goal is to train your ear and mouth to work together, not to prove you can keep up with a native speaker. Repeat the clip two or three times without the transcript. Each time, notice something different — once for rhythm, once for a specific sound, once to see how much you can anticipate before you hear it. Move on when: you can shadow the clip without needing to glance at the transcript. Step 5. Record Yourself, Compare, and Fix One Thing This is the step most people skip, and it is the one that creates actual improvement. Record yourself shadowing the clip. Then listen to the recording and compare it directly to the original audio. Do not try to fix everything at once. Each session, pick one specific thing: Word stress on a particular phrase The ending sound of a sentence An intonation pattern The reduction of a common word Repeat that section until the one thing you targeted sounds closer to the original. This is also where external feedback becomes genuinely useful. When you listen to your own recording, it can be difficult to hear exactly what is different — especially for sounds that do not exist in your first language. Your brain tends to hear what it expects rather than what is actually there. Getting External Feedback: Speechling When you genuinely cannot identify what is different between your recording and the original, self-comparison alone has a ceiling. This is where Speechling becomes useful. The core loop is simple: Speechling plays a sentence spoken by a native speaker, you record yourself saying the same thing, and the interface shows both waveforms side by side. The visual comparison often reveals rhythm and vowel length issues before your ear can catch them — you can see where your recording is compressed or rushed even if it sounds acceptable to you on playback. If you want more specific feedback, you can save a recording for coaching. A native speaker reviews it and sends back notes on exactly what is different — not a generic correction, but a response to your specific recording. A few things that make it practical for this method in particular: It supports Japanese and Korean alongside other languages, so it fits directly into the kind of material Language Finds readers are working with. Practice is organised by topic (weather, daily conversation, and so on), which means you can use it alongside the same content you are shadowing rather than switching to unrelated material. After each recording, you rate it as Hard, Okay, or Easy. The built-in spaced repetition system brings back sentences you struggle with more frequently, so you are not managing a separate review list. Speechling is not a substitute for the self-comparison step above — forming your own judgment about what is off is itself a skill worth developing. But when you are stuck and cannot name the gap, it gives you a concrete external reference instead of leaving you to guess. Practice your pronunciation with Speechling → Move on when: you have identified and corrected one noticeable difference between your recording and the original. A Real Shadowing Example Here is what the method looks like in practice. The clip contains this sentence: I didn’t really expect it to take this long, but I’m glad I stuck with it. First listen Ask yourself: what happened? Did I hear every word? You might catch expect , long , and glad , but miss stuck with it at natural speed. Check the transcript Look up what you missed. Notice expressions you recognise in print but did not catch in real time: expect it to , I’m glad I , stick with something . Shadow with the transcript Before shadowing, mark the sentence for stress: I didn’t REALLY expect it / to take this LONG / but I’m GLAD I stuck with it. Shadow two to three times, following those stress points rather than trying to copy every sound at once. Shadow without the transcript Close the text. Shadow the same sentence two or three times. You will probably fall slightly behind on stuck with it — that is fine. Keep the rhythm. Record Listen back. You notice that stuck with it comes out word by word instead of as a single connected phrase. That is your one thing to fix today. Repeat only that section until it sounds joined. Independent output Close everything. Now say: I didn’t expect learning Korean to take this long, but I’m glad I stuck with it. You have taken the original structure, replaced the content with something from your own life, and produced it without any audio playing. That is the transfer this method is designed to create. The Step Most Shadowing Guides Miss: Speak Without the Audio After you have shadowed and compared, do one more thing: close everything and speak on your own. Do not try to recite the clip. Instead, take the topic or situation the speaker was discussing and say something yourself. If the clip was someone explaining why they prefer working from home, your task is not to repeat their explanation. It is to answer the same question in your own words: Do you prefer working from home? Why or why not? Use whatever vocabulary and phrases from the clip felt natural. Ignore the rest. The point is to move from imitation to independent production — to detach the language from the original audio and attach it to your own thoughts. The sequence is simple: Shadow → Close → Recall → Reuse This is the step that converts shadowing practice into speaking ability. Without it, you are training a skill that only works when the audio is playing. Finish when: you can say something new using at least one expression from the clip. A 15-Minute Shadowing Routine If you want a practical structure you can use immediately: Time Activity 0:00 – 2:00 First listen (meaning only, no repeating) 2:00 – 5:00 Check transcript, mark unclear sections 5:00 – 9:00 Shadow with transcript, then without 9:00 – 12:00 Record yourself, listen back, fix one thing 12:00 – 15:00 Close everything, speak freely on the same topic A focused 15-minute session is often enough to work through one short clip without turning the exercise into passive repetition. If Shadowing Feels Too Hard, Do This Problem What to do I cannot keep up with the speaker Slow the audio slightly, or choose a shorter clip. Keeping up is not the goal — noticing the patterns is. I can read the transcript but cannot hear what I am reading Replay only the unclear sentence and listen alongside the transcript until the written and spoken forms match. I understand it, but my mouth cannot follow Switch temporarily to listen-and-repeat for that sentence. Once your mouth can reproduce it without real-time pressure, return to shadowing. I sound different but cannot work out why Compare one feature at a time — stress first, then vowel sounds, then endings. Speechling is useful here: record a phrase and receive feedback from a native speaker coach on what is different. I can shadow perfectly but still cannot speak independently Stop shadowing. Close the audio and do the 30-second independent output task. More shadowing is unlikely to solve this on its own — you need to practise speaking without the model. How to Choose Good Shadowing Material Choose Someone You Actually Want to Sound Like Most people pick material based on convenience rather than intention. Think about what register, accent, and speaking style you are aiming for, and choose a speaker who represents that. Use Short Clips A podcast episode is not a shadowing session. A 45-second excerpt from that podcast episode is. Shorter material allows you to go deeper — multiple passes, focused attention, real improvement on specific features. Stay Near Your Current Level Material that is slightly challenging is ideal. Material that is mostly incomprehensible is not a sign of ambition — it is a sign that the method will not work. If you cannot follow the meaning, there is much less useful language for you to notice, remember, and reuse. Prefer Audio With a Transcript Especially in the early stages. Transcripts let you verify what you heard and catch the gap between how a word is written and how it actually sounds. As your listening improves, you can shadow more material without transcripts. But there is no point in avoiding them early on. When Should You Stop Repeating a Clip? You do not need a clip to be perfect before moving on. Move to new material when: You understand the clip fully without the transcript Your rhythm and stress roughly match the original You have addressed the most noticeable pronunciation gap you identified You can reproduce the main ideas without the audio playing Holding onto a single clip for too long produces diminishing returns. The goal is not to master one short piece of audio. It is to use each clip to build habits that carry across to new material. Common Shadowing Mistakes Mistake Why it matters Choosing material that is too difficult If you cannot follow the meaning, you are chasing sounds rather than acquiring language. Shadowing too long a clip Longer is not better. A short clip worked through carefully produces more than a long one done passively. Chasing synchronisation Matching the speaker perfectly is not the goal. Noticing and internalising patterns is. Skipping the recording step It is difficult to assess your pronunciation accurately while you are speaking. You need the playback. Never speaking independently If every session ends with the audio still on, you are practising imitation, not fluency. Frequently Asked Questions Does shadowing really improve speaking? It improves specific aspects of speaking — pronunciation, rhythm, intonation, and the ability to produce sounds at natural speed. It does not automatically improve your ability to construct sentences or express your own ideas. For that, you need the independent output step described above. How long should I shadow each day? Fifteen to twenty focused minutes is plenty for a daily session. Consistency matters more than making each session long, and a short routine is easier to repeat regularly. Is shadowing good for beginners? It depends on the material. Complete beginners who have no listening foundation yet will struggle, because shadowing requires you to process meaning and produce sound simultaneously. If you are at a very early stage, spend time building listening comprehension first. Once you can follow simple audio, shadowing becomes useful. Should I shadow with or without subtitles? For the first pass, use the transcript to check comprehension. Then shadow without it. Reading while shadowing splits your attention and tends to train your eyes more than your ears. How many times should I repeat the same audio? For a short clip, a few focused passes are usually enough. Stop when you are no longer noticing useful differences. If you shadow the same clip across multiple days, you will notice your attention to detail improving — you will catch things on day three that you missed on day one. Can I use movies, dramas, podcasts, or YouTube for shadowing? All of these work. Drama dialogue is particularly useful because it tends to be clear, emotionally varied, and contextually rich. Podcasts work well if the speaker has a natural but not excessively fast delivery. Whatever you choose, make sure the audio quality is clean enough to hear connected speech clearly. Final Thoughts Shadowing is best treated as a bridge. It helps you move from hearing a language to reproducing its rhythm, stress, and pronunciation. But the bridge only goes somewhere if you take the last step: close the audio, close the transcript, and try to say something yourself. The speakers you shadow have spent years building the intuitions you are trying to develop. You are not going to absorb those intuitions by repeating after them with the audio still playing. At some point, you have to let go of the model and trust what you have built. Listen. Notice. Imitate. Compare. Reuse. That sequence — done consistently, with short material at the right level — is what actually moves the language from something you can copy into something you can use. Enjoyed this guide? title: TEUIDA vs LingoDeer for Korean: Speaking or Grammar?
text: TEUIDA vs LingoDeer for Korean: Speaking or Grammar First? Choose around your next learning task: speaking aloud, understanding sentence patterns, or building a routine. Here is what official descriptions and learner discussions reveal. October 22, 2026 Korean Start by considering TEUIDA if your main difficulty is getting yourself to speak Korean aloud. Start by considering LingoDeer if you want a course that explains how Korean sentences fit together. Before paying, try the activity you expect to repeat most often—not just the one that makes the best first impression. That recommendation follows their stated teaching approaches. It does not mean TEUIDA teaches no grammar, or that LingoDeer offers no speaking practice. Their emphasis is the more useful starting point for comparison. This guide uses official product descriptions and linked learner discussions checked on October 22, 2026. We have not completed either Korean course or independently measured their pronunciation feedback. TEUIDA vs LingoDeer at a glance What you need next Start by considering What to check in a sample A reason to answer aloud TEUIDA Whether its conversation scenarios make you produce an answer. Clear explanations of sentence patterns LingoDeer Whether you can explain and reuse the pattern after a lesson. Feedback while practising pronunciation TEUIDA Whether the feedback tells you what to change. A grammar-based learning sequence LingoDeer Whether the lesson order and explanations suit your pace. A sustainable daily routine Either Whether you can repeat the activity in your real study environment. The best choice depends partly on what is already in your routine. An app can be useful as a supplement even when it would not be your preferred main course. What TEUIDA emphasizes TEUIDA's official site emphasizes speaking from the beginning, real-life conversation scenarios, interactive lessons, and pronunciation feedback. Its homepage describes AI pronunciation analysis. TEUIDA’s public website demonstrates an interactive Korean lesson and describes pronunciation feedback. The app preview is supplied by TEUIDA; it is not our own lesson result. Official website screenshot, October 22, 2026. Source . For a beginner who understands a phrase but hesitates to say it, a scenario can provide a concrete prompt: someone expects an answer, and your task is to respond aloud. The key question is what that prompt gets you to do. Do you construct an answer, repeat a model, or rely on a hint? All can be useful activities, but they are different demands. During a sample, notice which one you are practising. Also consider where you will use it. A speaking activity may fit a quiet room much better than a commute where you cannot comfortably talk into your phone. The strongest lesson is not useful if your usual study setting makes you skip it. What LingoDeer emphasizes LingoDeer's official site describes a grammar-based curriculum, detailed explanations, review activities, native-speaker audio, and stories with speaking practice. The “Why LingoDeer?” section describes the broader product’s curriculum and practice features; it does not verify the contents of every Korean lesson. Official website screenshot, October 22, 2026. Source . That makes it worth investigating if you dislike guessing your way through exercises. A learner may need to know why a particle or ending appears before practising it in several sentences. An explanation is only the beginning, though. After reading one, check whether you can do something with it. Can you recognize the pattern in a new sentence? Can you change a simple detail without copying the example? The homepage describes the broader product. It does not establish that every language course contains identical material or reaches the same depth. Evaluate the Korean course specifically rather than relying on a recommendation written about a different language. What Korean learners say about TEUIDA A December 2023 discussion in r/Korean asked which app was worth a beginner's time and money. The replies are useful because they focus on particular experiences rather than a simple winner. One learner described TEUIDA as helping them study consistently after previous attempts at Korean had stalled. That is a reason to investigate whether its format helps you start speaking and return the next day. Another learner liked the course but wanted more content . Their comment concerns the course available at the time. It is a prompt to check today's curriculum, not evidence that the current app ends at the same point. The thread also contains conflicting experiences of speech recognition. Some found answers difficult to register; others felt it worked well or described changing their pronunciation. These accounts cannot establish the system's accuracy. They do show why a trial should include the sounds and sentences you find difficult. What those comments do—and do not—tell us about LingoDeer The Korean thread contains users with different levels of experience in each app. Some explicitly say they have used only one. Their comments should not be treated as a matched comparison of both complete courses. It also mentions LingoDeer Plus , which a commenter describes as a practice app. Do not assume a recommendation for Plus is a review of the main LingoDeer course, or that purchasing one automatically answers questions about the other. Check the current product and plan details. A separate Japanese-learning comment praises LingoDeer's more explicit explanations and describes later moving to Genki. That is an illustration of what someone valued in the teaching style. It is not evidence that the Korean course delivers the same outcome. For Korean, use these accounts to decide what to inspect yourself: explanation, practice, pacing, and the next step after a lesson. How to compare them around one small task Use a beginner task you care about, such as introducing yourself or answering a simple everyday question. Find relevant sample material in each app, where available. Then compare the experience rather than the score: Notice whether you understand the meaning and sentence structure. Answer before looking at the model when the activity allows it. Check what happens after an incorrect or unclear answer. Return later and see whether you can produce something without the same prompts. This is a suggested selection exercise, not a test we have performed. Its purpose is to expose the gap between enjoying a lesson and knowing what to do next. You may discover that you like one app's explanation but prefer the other's speaking prompts. That does not mean you need two subscriptions immediately. First check whether an existing resource already covers one of those jobs. Treat pronunciation scores as feedback to investigate An accepted answer can feel encouraging. A rejected one can feel personal. Neither response, by itself, tells you how well a person would understand you in a conversation. When trying TEUIDA, look for useful information: does it help you notice a particular sound or phrase? Can you understand what to change? Does trying again become clearer, or do you find yourself chasing acceptance without knowing why? If the result seems inconsistent, try again in a quiet setting and compare with the model audio. For a sound that remains confusing, an explanation or feedback from a qualified teacher may answer a question that an app score cannot. There is no need to infer a diagnosis from a Reddit comment or a single recording. Before paying, check the current course and plan Open the current curriculum and access information for your device and region. Look at the activities you want, how far the course extends, what a trial includes, and what happens when it ends. Check renewal, cancellation, and any refund terms before committing. This article does not repeat old discount amounts or assume that a historical lifetime offer is still available. Also ask what you will use after the app. If you need more explicit study, How to Study Korean is a resource to investigate. For another form of reading practice, explore StoryKorean . Our Korean YouTube guide offers additional directions for finding explanations and listening material. Choose a supplement only when you can name the job it will do. Questions beginners ask Is TEUIDA or LingoDeer better for a complete beginner? TEUIDA is worth trying when you need structured prompts to speak. LingoDeer is worth trying when understanding grammar is your immediate need. Your study setting and response to the lesson format matter as much as the feature list. Should I buy both? Start with one clear gap. If you already have a grammar course, you may want speaking practice. If you have listening and speaking material but cannot understand the sentence patterns, explanations may be more useful. You can reconsider after establishing a routine. Does a high pronunciation score mean I can speak Korean well? It shows how an app evaluated a particular attempt. It does not establish your ability to understand an unfamiliar question, choose an appropriate response, or maintain a conversation. How should I make the final choice? Repeat a small activity on more than one day. Keep the option that helps you understand what you are practising, gives you a useful next step, and fits a routine you can maintain. Sources TEUIDA official homepage : stated teaching emphasis, checked October 22, 2026. LingoDeer official homepage : stated curriculum and practice features, checked October 22, 2026.
