title: Todaii Review (2026): Is It Worth It for Japanese Learners?
text: Todaii Japanese Review (2026): Is It Worth It? I have been looking for a Japanese reading site I can actually stick with long-term. My requirements were specific: fresh content updated regularly, topics that do not feel like a textbook, easy word lookup, and ideally some vocabulary and grammar support built in. Todaii Japanese ticks most of those boxes. I spent time going through… August 13, 2026 Japanese Key Takeaways This Todaii Japanese review covers everything you need to know before trying the app, from free vs paid to how it fits into a daily study routine. Todaii Japanese offers daily Japanese reading content graded from N5 to N1, with vocabulary, grammar notes, and JLPT practice built into every article. The free version is enough for most self-study learners who read one to three articles per day. The biggest limitation is ads on the free version; the audio in flashcards is AI-generated and not suited for shadowing practice. I have been looking for a Japanese reading site I can actually stick with long-term. My requirements were specific: fresh content updated regularly, topics that do not feel like a textbook, easy word lookup, and ideally some vocabulary and grammar support built in. Todaii Japanese ticks most of those boxes. I spent time going through almost every feature on the site, and this review covers what I found — what works, what does not, and whether the free version is enough. My verdict: the free version covers most of what self-study learners actually need. The paid version is worth considering only if you hit the daily limits consistently. Quick Overview Feature Detail 👤 Best for Intermediate to advanced learners (N3 and above) 🆓 Free version Enough for 1–3 articles per day 💰 Paid version Removes ads, unlocks unlimited reading 📰 Content Daily updated news, graded N5–N1 📱 Platforms Web, iOS, Android ✅ Biggest strength Real Japanese content with built-in vocab and grammar tools ❌ Biggest weakness Ads on free version; AI audio not suited for shadowing What Is Todaii Japanese? Todaii Japanese is a web and mobile app that aggregates Japanese news and cultural content, grades it by JLPT difficulty, and wraps it in a set of study tools: vocabulary lists, grammar notes, flashcards, a dictionary, and mock tests. It is not a course. There is no fixed syllabus or lesson sequence. The idea is closer to: find something you want to read in Japanese, read it, and let the built-in tools help you study what you just encountered. That approach suits some learners very well and others not at all. If you want a structured grammar curriculum, Todaii is not the right tool. If you want daily exposure to real Japanese content with study support built in, it is one of the better free options available. The site is available at japanese.todaiinews.com . What I Tested I went through most of the main features on the web version: Daily news articles at different JLPT levels Vocabulary and grammar notes inside articles Flashcard system JLPT vocabulary library Video module Word Sorting exercises JLPT mock tests Course and idiom content Here is what I found. 1. Daily Updated Content — The Most Important Feature This is the feature I care about most, and Todaii does it well. The articles are not a fixed library that sits unchanged for years. New content goes up every day, and the topics are chosen to be genuinely interesting rather than textbook-safe. When I was using it, articles included things like why changes in weather make your body feel tired, why you rinse your hands at a shrine, and news about a volcano eruption. These are real topics that make you want to click in, not reading comprehension passages engineered to use N3 grammar points. For me, this matters more than most other features. A reading app with beautiful design but content I have no interest in reading will not get opened. Todaii consistently gives me a reason to come back. This also makes it a strong NHK Web Easy alternative for learners who want more variety in their reading material and topic selection. 2. JLPT Level Filtering Every article on Todaii is labeled with a JLPT difficulty level, from N5 through N1. You can filter by level, by topic, or both. This gives you two different ways to use the site: The first is level-first: pick your target level and find articles to practice with. This is useful if you are actively preparing for JLPT and want reading material that matches your exam target. The second is topic-first: find a subject you actually want to read about, then check what level the article sits at. If the topic is interesting enough, it is often worth attempting an article slightly above your comfortable level. I prefer the second approach. It keeps the learning feeling less deliberate, which for me makes it easier to stay consistent. 3. Highlight Words Without Leaving the Article One of the features I use most while reading is Todaii’s built-in word lookup. You can highlight a word without leaving the article, and a lookup panel opens with the reading, part of speech, English definitions, and pronunciation. From there, you can also save the word directly to your vocabulary list for later review. The panel separates Vocabulary, Kanji, and Sentence information, and furigana can be displayed throughout the article. This makes it easy to check a word quickly and keep reading without constantly switching to another dictionary. The example sentences in the lookup panel do not appear to have audio, which is one limitation. They do include furigana, though, so they are still useful for seeing how a word works in context. For me, the most useful part is how little this interrupts the reading flow: Highlight a word → Check the reading and meaning → Listen to pronunciation → Save it if useful → Keep reading 4. Vocabulary and Grammar After Each Article Todaii’s study support continues after you finish reading. Each article is followed by vocabulary, grammar points, and practice questions based on the text you have just read. For example, after reading an article about weather and fatigue, the grammar section highlighted the pattern 〜によって and explained it using a sentence from the article: 内耳が気圧の変化を感じ取ることによって引き起こされるといいます。 I like this approach because the grammar does not appear in isolation. I have already seen the sentence inside a real article, so when Todaii explains 〜によって , I already understand the situation in which it was used. The post-reading flow is simple: Finish the article → Review vocabulary → Study grammar → Do practice questions → Review saved words with flashcards This is one of the things I like most about Todaii. An article does not end when I reach the last sentence. The vocabulary and grammar I have just encountered immediately become material for review. If you already make notes while reading Japanese content, the process will probably feel familiar. Todaii simply keeps more of that workflow inside the same platform. 5. Flashcards — Useful, But Watch the Audio Words from any article can be saved directly to Todaii’s flashcard system. Each card shows the word, reading, JLPT level, part of speech, English definition, and audio. You mark each card as Not Memorized, Not Sure, or Memorized. The system works smoothly, and going straight from encountering a word in an article to having it in a review deck is a convenience that actually gets used. One limitation worth noting: the audio in the flashcards has a noticeable AI quality. It is accurate enough for checking a reading, but I would not use it for shadowing or accent training. For that, I use the video module instead. 6. JLPT Vocabulary Library — A Genuinely Useful Free Resource I did not expect much from this section, but it turned out to be one of the most useful parts of the site. Todaii has dedicated vocabulary lists for all five JLPT levels: Level Vocabulary Count N5 578 N4 512 N3 1,553 N2 1,560 N1 2,753 Source: Todaii Japanese vocabulary library, checked August 2026. The main JLPT vocabulary lists are available for free. Individual entries can include readings, definitions, usage notes, and memory tips, and words can also be saved to flashcards for later review. Beyond the five JLPT levels, Todaii also has topic-specific vocabulary lists covering Japanese particles, prefixes, suffixes, fixed expressions, onomatopoeia, common connectives for reading comprehension, homophones, and kanji with the same kun reading. For JLPT learners, I think this is one of the strongest free parts of Todaii. Even if you mainly use the site for reading practice, the vocabulary library is useful as a separate reference when you want to review words by level or category. 7. Video Module — Better for Listening Than Flashcards Todaii includes news video clips from sources like ANN and ABEMA News, with Japanese subtitles displayed alongside the video. Most clips are one to three minutes long. The video library does not appear to be actively updated — the most recent content I found was from several years ago. That said, the existing archive is large enough that finding useful practice material is not a problem. Because the audio comes from real broadcasts rather than generated speech, this is where I go when I want to practice listening or work on natural intonation — not the flashcard audio. My approach for a short video: First listen without looking at the subtitles Second listen with subtitles Identify two or three expressions I did not catch Repeat those sections For learners who find 20-minute podcasts hard to fit into a day, one or two of these short clips can be a more sustainable daily listening habit. 8. Word Sorting — Skip If You Read Chinese Todaii includes a Word Sorting exercise where you rearrange scrambled kanji to form a word. For learners without a Chinese background, this probably builds useful recognition of kanji combinations. For readers already comfortable with Chinese characters, many of these exercises may feel very easy. If you encounter a pure-kanji sorting exercise, just skip it and move on. 9. Japanese Courses, Idioms, and Folk Tales Todaii goes further than most reading apps with additional content categories: Grammar lessons Conversation lessons Idioms (慣用語): expressions like 鼻が高い, 腹が黒い, 三日坊主 Japanese folk tales: 桃太郎, 花咲かじいさん, and others Difference comparisons between similar words or grammar Some of this is free, some requires a paid plan. My approach: use whatever is not locked, skip what is. 10. JLPT Mock Tests Todaii includes N5 through N1 mock tests. On Todaii’s platform, each mock test is set at 80 questions over 105 minutes — note this is Todaii’s own format, not the official JLPT exam structure, which varies by level. Mock Test 1 and 2 are free. Tests 3 through 10 require a paid subscription. Source: Todaii Japanese JLPT test page , checked August 2026. For occasional level-checking or a taste of JLPT format, the free tests are enough. If you are in intensive exam preparation and need to cycle through many full practice tests, the paid access becomes more relevant. The Main Problem With the Free Version: Ads The most noticeable downside of the free version is the advertising. On the web version, some banner ads are large enough to interrupt reading flow. When you are trying to move between an article, a vocabulary list, a grammar explanation, and a practice question, a prominent ad appearing mid-page breaks concentration. The paid plan removes all ads. This is the most practical reason to upgrade if you use Todaii daily for focused study. The free version also limits daily reading to around three articles. For most self-study learners, one to three articles read carefully is already a solid session. But if you want to read more, you will hit the limit. Is Todaii Worth It? Free vs Paid Feature Free Paid Daily articles Limited (~3) Unlimited JLPT vocabulary library Most content free Full access Flashcards Available Available Video module Available Available Mock tests Tests 1–2 Tests 1–10 Ads Yes Removed Courses and idioms Partial Full access My take: The free version is enough for most learners who read one to three articles per day and use the vocabulary and grammar tools after each one. The paid version makes sense if you study for long sessions daily and find the ads genuinely disruptive. Who Is Todaii Japanese Best For? Good fit: N3 and above learners who want daily Japanese reading practice Learners who prefer topic-driven content over textbook exercises Anyone preparing for JLPT who wants free graded reading material Learners who want vocabulary and grammar support without switching apps Less suited for: Absolute beginners who have not started grammar yet Learners who want a fixed lesson sequence or curriculum Learners who rely heavily on audio for pronunciation or shadowing practice How I Use Todaii Alongside Other Resources I mainly use Todaii as a reading tool rather than trying to make it cover every part of Japanese study. For me, it works better when I pair it with resources that give me more listening and video-based input. For Listening Practice: Japanese Podcasts For longer listening practice, I usually switch to Japanese podcasts. This gives me a different kind of exposure from Todaii. Instead of stopping to study every unfamiliar word, I can listen for expressions I already know, notice how vocabulary sounds in natural speech, and get used to following Japanese without relying on written text all the time. If you are looking for something that matches your level, I put together a separate guide to the 15 Best Japanese Podcasts by Level (2026) . For Learning Through Shows: Lingopie When I want something more visual than a podcast, I use Lingopie . Start Learning Japanese for Free Lingopie turns shows and videos into interactive study material. Instead of watching passively, I can use the subtitles to look up vocabulary, save useful words, replay difficult lines, and return to what I learned later. Feature Why I Find It Useful Dual subtitles Follow the Japanese while keeping an English translation available when needed Clickable vocabulary Look up unfamiliar words directly from the subtitles without leaving the video Save to vocabulary Keep useful words in a personal vocabulary list for later review Replay and playback controls Go back to dialogue I did not catch and listen again more slowly Flashcards and review Revisit vocabulary after watching instead of forgetting it when the episode ends Pronunciation practice Use the original dialogue as a model for listening and repeating I use Todaii and Lingopie for different reasons. Todaii is where I slow down and read carefully; Lingopie is where I learn from video and connect vocabulary with natural speech, subtitles, and context. Learning Japanese with Shows What I like most is that vocabulary practice starts before the video even begins. Lingopie first shows a set of words matched to the video and my level, and I can choose which ones I want to add before watching. While the video is playing, I can also click unfamiliar words in the subtitles and save them to My Vocab . Those words can then be reviewed later through spaced-repetition exercises, so the vocabulary does not disappear when the episode ends. That creates a simple learning loop: Preview vocabulary → Watch → Look up new words → Save to My Vocab → Review → Return to the video Together with Japanese podcasts, this gives me a balanced mix of reading, natural listening, video-based learning, and vocabulary review without asking one tool to do everything. Todaii Japanese Review FAQs Is Todaii Japanese free? Yes. Todaii Japanese has a free version with daily article limits and ads. Most of the vocabulary library, flashcard system, video module, and the first two mock tests are available without paying. What level is Todaii Japanese for? Todaii works best for learners at N3 level and above. Content is available at all levels from N5 to N1, but beginners who have not yet covered basic grammar may find it difficult to use effectively without additional support. Is Todaii Japanese better than NHK Web Easy? They serve similar purposes but with differences. NHK Web Easy focuses on simplified news with furigana. Todaii pulls from a wider range of sources and topics, and adds vocabulary, grammar notes, flashcards, and mock tests. For learners who want more study tools alongside their reading, Todaii offers more in one place. Does Todaii Japanese have an app? Yes. Todaii Japanese is available on iOS and Android as well as the web version at japanese.todaiinews.com. Is Todaii Japanese worth paying for? The paid version is worth it if you study for long daily sessions and find the ads disruptive, or if you need unlimited article access beyond the free daily limit. For most self-study learners reading one to three articles per day, the free version is sufficient. Final Thoughts Todaii Japanese is one of the most complete free tools available for intermediate Japanese learners who want to build a daily reading habit with real content. The combination of daily updated articles, JLPT grading, built-in vocabulary and grammar support, and a free vocabulary library makes it genuinely useful — not just a novelty app. The ads on the free version are a real inconvenience during focused study. But the content itself is good enough that I keep coming back. If you are at N3 or above and looking for a site that gives you something new and interesting to read in Japanese every day, Todaii Japanese is worth trying. Last checked: August 2026. You can replay the sound, switch between scripts and use the same Basic, Voiced, Combinations and All kana levels. Practice kana listening ↑ Play sound か き く け Choose the Kana You’re Ready to Practice Keep the first round manageable, then expand the character set when recognition feels comfortable. Basic 46 Start with the core hiragana or katakana. Voiced Add dakuten and handakuten forms such as が, ざ, ば and ぱ. Combinations Practice yōon such as きゃ, しゅ and ちょ. All kana Mix every available level into one challenge. Practice Confusing Katakana Characters Katakana characters can look nearly identical when you first meet them. Look-alike Lab gives troublesome pairs their own focused practice instead of hiding them inside a full kana chart. Compare stroke direction, answer the pair repeatedly and use the review list to see exactly what still needs practice. Practice tricky katakana ↑ シ vs ツ more horizontal · more vertical ソ vs ン compare the starting stroke and long sweep Practice Common Katakana Words Knowing カ, メ and ラ separately does not always mean you can immediately read カメラ. Katakana becomes more useful when you meet it inside complete words. Word Meaning trains katakana-to-English reading, Build the Word reverses the direction, and Katakana 100+ gives you fifteen scored vocabulary sets. Take the Katakana 100+ challenge Practice 150 words across food, travel, technology, home, school, health, music, people and other everyday themes. Practice katakana words ↑ テレビ television コンビニ convenience store ホテル hotel スマホ smartphone レストラン restaurant How to Practice Kana Effectively Start with accuracy Learn hiragana first, work through one row at a time, and say each sound aloud before choosing an answer. Add sound and contrast Use Sound Match and Look-alike Lab to connect what you hear with what you see and isolate recurring mistakes. Graduate to words Once recognition feels comfortable, practice small kana, doubled consonants and long vowels inside useful katakana words. Where Faster Kana Reading Helps Short kana practice becomes useful when Japanese appears outside a study chart. Read katakana on menus and signs while traveling. Recognize names and titles in anime credits. Navigate Japanese game menus with less hesitation. Build faster recognition for beginner reading tests. Fit a focused round into a short commute or study break. More Kana Practice Questions Can complete beginners use this kana game? Yes. Begin with Basic 46 and choose Hiragana. Add Katakana, listening and mixed practice after the first characters become familiar. Can I practice dakuten and combination kana? Yes. Choose Voiced for dakuten and handakuten forms, Combinations for yōon such as きゃ and しゅ, or All kana to mix every available level. Can I practice kana by listening? Yes. Sound Match plays a Japanese pronunciation first and asks you to choose the matching kana. The voice is provided by your browser’s Japanese speech system. When should I stop relying on romaji? Use romaji to confirm sounds at the beginning, then spend more time matching kana directly to sound and reading complete words. Are all the games multiple choice? The answer controls use choices, but the task changes between speed recognition, sound-first matching, two-way look-alike practice, word meaning and meaning-to-katakana recall. Japanese Kana Game FAQ What is kana in Japanese? Kana is the name for Japan’s two sound-based scripts: hiragana and katakana. Each character represents a mora, a short rhythmic sound unit. Kanji mainly carry meaning, while romaji writes Japanese sounds with the Latin alphabet. What is the difference between hiragana and katakana? Both scripts represent the same basic Japanese sounds. Hiragana is common in grammar and native Japanese words, while katakana is often used for loanwords, foreign names, sound effects, emphasis and specialist terms. Should I learn hiragana or katakana first? Most beginners start with hiragana because it appears throughout beginner Japanese. Learn katakana soon afterwards, then mix both scripts once you can recognize them separately. How can I remember katakana more easily? Combine short character drills with listening, comparisons of similar shapes and real-word practice. Seeing the same kana inside familiar words creates more useful memory cues than repeating a chart alone. Why is katakana harder to read? Learners often see it less frequently, several characters have similar shapes, and borrowed words change to fit Japanese pronunciation. Practicing both individual kana and complete words addresses all three problems. How long does it take to learn kana? The pace varies, but short daily sessions are more useful than one long cram. Track both accuracy and recognition speed, then move to words when the basic characters no longer require slow decoding. How can I tell シ and ツ apart? Compare their stroke direction: the short marks in シ are arranged more horizontally, while those in ツ fall more vertically. Look-alike Lab lets you practice the contrast directly. How can I tell ソ and ン apart? Focus on the starting direction of the short stroke and the angle of the long curved stroke. Alternating the pair in a quiz helps your eye learn the difference. What is included in the Katakana 100+ test? It is a 150-word katakana quiz divided into fifteen themed sets of ten. Each round scores your reading and meaning recognition out of ten and saves the best result for that set. Will my progress be saved? Your best score for each game and each Katakana 100+ set is stored locally in your browser. No account is required. Go From Recognizing Kana to Reading Real Words Choose the skill that slows you down and play another focused round. Play a Japanese Kana Game ↑

title: YUYUの日本語Podcast Review: 3+ Years of Listening
text: YUYUの日本語Podcast Review: Is It Good for N3–N2 Learners? This YUYUの日本語Podcast review is based on three to four years of listening and probably hundreds of episodes. I first started listening because Japanese listening made up a big part of my study routine, but YUYU gradually became one of the few podcasts I still open even when I am not particularly in the mood to… August 20, 2026 Japanese This YUYUの日本語Podcast review is based on three to four years of listening and probably hundreds of episodes. I first started listening because Japanese listening made up a big part of my study routine, but YUYU gradually became one of the few podcasts I still open even when I am not particularly in the mood to “study.” The balance is what keeps me coming back. YUYU speaks at a pace that feels fairly close to everyday Japanese conversation, but his pronunciation is very clear. When he uses a word or idea that may be difficult, he often explains it again in simpler Japanese instead of immediately translating it. I also genuinely enjoy him as a host. He is funny, his topics move from Japanese learning and movies to daily life and culture, and a seemingly casual story can sometimes turn into a surprisingly thoughtful discussion. For learners around JLPT N3–N2 , YUYU is one of my strongest Japanese podcast recommendations. ⭐ Quick Verdict My Take Overall rating ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Best level N3–N2 Speaking speed Close to everyday Japanese Pronunciation Very clear Episode length Often around 20–40 minutes Best for Listening, shadowing, conversational Japanese Beginner friendly ⭐⭐⭐☆☆ Topic variety ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ YouTube study value ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Patreon Worth it for active study Best for: Intermediate learners ready to move beyond very slow learner Japanese. My favorite thing: YUYU makes harder Japanese understandable without making the Japanese sound unnaturally slow. I compared more beginner, intermediate, and advanced options in my guide to the best Japanese podcasts for learners . 🎧 What Level Is YUYUの日本語Podcast? I would place YUYU around N3–N2 , with N3 being the point where I think the podcast becomes especially useful. The main difficulty is not unusually fast speech. It is being able to follow one topic in Japanese for 20, 30, or sometimes 40 minutes without stopping every time you hear an unfamiliar word. Level My Take How I’d Use YUYU N4 Challenging Short clips + transcript support N3 ⭐ Sweet spot Full episodes + active listening N2 Very comfortable Natural expressions + shadowing N1+ Easy to follow Casual immersion + phrasing N4: Use Short Sections First A learner around N4 may understand many individual sentences and still lose the overall thread. You hear one unknown word, start translating it in your head, and suddenly YUYU is already several sentences ahead. That is why I would not call this a true beginner podcast even though his pronunciation is very clear. Short sections work much better at this stage. One to five minutes is enough to practice without turning a full episode into an endurance test. N3: The Sweet Spot Around N3, YUYU becomes difficult in a productive way. You can normally understand enough to stay with the topic, while still encountering useful vocabulary, casual grammar, sentence endings, and expressions that do not always appear in beginner textbooks. That balance matters. Too difficult, and you spend the whole episode lost. Too easy, and there is little left to notice. YUYU sits nicely in the middle. N2 and Above: Focus on How He Speaks At N2 and above, the question becomes less: Can I understand this sentence? and more: How would I say this naturally? I pay more attention to how YUYU connects ideas, softens an opinion, changes sentence endings, paraphrases something difficult, and moves between a personal story and a broader point. That makes the podcast useful long after basic comprehension stops being the main challenge. 💬 Why I’ve Kept Listening for 3–4 Years Plenty of Japanese learner podcasts are useful for a few weeks. Far fewer are interesting enough to stay in my routine for years. YUYU works for me because the Japanese, the content, and his personality all help at the same time. 1. Natural Speed, Clear Pronunciation YUYU does not sound like someone reading beginner Japanese word by word. His pace feels fairly close to normal conversation, but he articulates very clearly. I can usually separate the sounds even when I do not know every word. That makes him a useful bridge: slow learner Japanese → YUYU → native podcasts The jump feels much smaller than moving directly from heavily controlled beginner audio to a fast native conversation. 2. He Paraphrases Difficult Japanese This is probably the feature I notice most as a learner. When YUYU thinks a word may be difficult, he often explains it again using easier Japanese. He may give another expression, add an example, or restate the idea before continuing. The pattern often feels like: difficult word → simpler Japanese → example/context → understanding That means I can keep processing the meaning in Japanese instead of immediately switching to Chinese or English. YUYU is easy to follow not because he only uses easy words, but because he knows how to make difficult Japanese understandable . 3. He Feels More Like a Person Than a Textbook YUYU jokes, reacts to his own stories, goes off on small tangents, and does not sound as though he is permanently in teacher mode. Sometimes it feels closer to listening to a friendly person talk about whatever has been on his mind recently. His voice is also very easy for me to listen to. It is clear, warm, and slightly soft, with a bit of that 優しい feeling that works surprisingly well for longer episodes. That is subjective, but after hundreds of episodes I no longer think liking someone’s voice is a trivial detail. A listening resource only works long term when you actually want to hear the person speak. 4. The Topics Are Light but Varied YUYU covers much more than Japanese grammar. Common topics include: Japanese learning music and movies anime travel everyday life Japanese culture personal experiences habits and relationships broader life reflections One episode can be practical and study-focused. The next can be about a cultural topic or something that happened in his own life. That variety is one of the reasons I have not become bored after so many episodes. 5. Casual Topics Often Lead Somewhere Deeper This is probably my favorite part of his content. YUYU often begins with something small that happened to him, then uses it to introduce the real topic. By the end, the conversation may have moved into happiness, habits, relationships, learning, or the way he thinks about life. The structure often feels like: personal experience → main topic → examples and thoughts → wrap-up Once I noticed that pattern, longer episodes became easier to follow too. Instead of treating every sentence like a separate listening test, I started listening for where the discussion was going. 6. He Updates Frequently Another underrated advantage is simply having enough new material. YUYU updates frequently and covers different subjects, so there is usually something new I want to play. That makes listening easier to turn into a routine. I do not need to search for a new Japanese resource every morning. I can open the channel, choose a topic that sounds interesting, and start listening. 🎥 The YouTube Channel Is Excellent for Studying I personally prefer the videos where YUYU appears on camera. Seeing his facial expressions and gestures gives me extra context, keeps me more engaged during a longer monologue, and helps when I want to imitate the way he actually delivers a sentence. The YUYUの日本語Podcast YouTube channel also does something I really appreciate: many of the talking-head videos include Japanese subtitles directly on screen . That is surprisingly useful. I can follow this sequence without leaving the video: listen → check the Japanese subtitle → listen again → shadow I do not need an English translation every time I miss something. For shadowing, seeing YUYU also lets me notice more than pronunciation: pauses rhythm emphasis facial expression where he speeds up or slows down how his delivery changes with the meaning My full guide to shadowing for language learning explains the listen → check → imitate → reuse process in more detail. 🧠 What I’ve Actually Learned From YUYU One reason I rate YUYU so highly is that the content itself often contains useful language-learning advice. I do not only get Japanese input from the episodes. Some of his ideas have changed how I study. Episode 1: Stop Trying to Understand Every Word One episode about understanding Japanese conversation changed how I think about listening. I used to treat listening like a test. Missing one word felt like failing the sentence. But real conversations are messy. People repeat themselves, change direction, add unnecessary details, go off topic, and sometimes do not even know exactly what they want to say when they begin. Trying to understand 100% of every word is not a realistic goal. The four ideas I kept from that episode: Find the topic first. Work out what the person is talking about before worrying about every unknown word. Predict what comes next. Context gives you possible vocabulary and ideas before you hear them. Listen selectively. The main message matters more than catching every side comment. Notice signposts. Expressions such as つまり , 僕の言いたいことは , and これ大事なポイントなんだけど tell you where to focus. A practice idea I liked was starting a Japanese livestream or podcast midway through and seeing how quickly I could identify the topic. 🔔 What I changed: I now judge listening by whether I can follow the speaker’s message, not by whether I caught every word. Episode 2: Can You Really Learn Japanese From Anime? I originally became interested in Japanese partly because of anime, so this topic felt very familiar. The embarrassing part is that after watching anime for years, I am not sure all those hours improved my Japanese as much as I once imagined. A lot of the time, I was doing this: eyes on Chinese subtitles → understand through the visuals → barely process the Japanese I could understand the story while listening surprisingly little. YUYU’s point was not that anime cannot teach Japanese. It was that what you should learn from anime changes with your level . Level What to Focus On Beginner Connect words with their sounds Intermediate Grammar, sentence endings, verb forms Advanced Word choice, tone, pronunciation, character voice For beginners, recognizing a word you already studied when a character says it is useful progress. At intermediate level, grammar becomes more interesting. You can notice casual verb forms, contractions, sentence endings, and when particular structures appear. Advanced learners can look more closely at nuance: why one character chooses a particular word, how personality affects speech, and what intonation adds to a line. My Three-Watch Method I like giving each watch a different purpose. First watch: understand the story. Use subtitles when necessary and enjoy the episode. Second watch: turn the subtitles off. Check whether you can still follow the overall meaning. Third watch: focus on the Japanese. Notice vocabulary, grammar, endings, pronunciation, and tone. This feels much more useful than vaguely telling myself to “learn Japanese from anime.” Episode 3: Turning Passive Vocabulary Into Active Vocabulary Another YUYU video I really liked is 「使える単語の増やし方 / How to Turn Passive Vocabulary into Active Vocabulary」 . The main distinction is simple but useful: Vocabulary Type What It Means Unknown vocabulary I do not understand it yet Passive vocabulary I understand it but cannot easily use it Active vocabulary I understand it and can use it myself This explains something I experience constantly. Recognizing a word and producing that word are different skills. I use a similar distinction in my own approach to learning Japanese vocabulary , especially when separating recognition from active recall and use. YUYU suggests several ways to move words toward active vocabulary. 1. Learn Vocabulary by Topic Words are easier to retrieve when they belong to a context. Cooking vocabulary, for example, becomes more useful when learned around the same topic instead of being mixed randomly with unrelated words. The material you consume also shapes the vocabulary you encounter. Someone who wants to talk about cooking needs different input from someone trying to understand Japanese news. 2. Keep Your Active Vocabulary Target Small One idea from the video is to learn more vocabulary for recognition than for active use. YUYU gives an example of roughly 15 words for understanding and five words for active use per day . I like the distinction more than the exact number. Trying to force every new word into active vocabulary creates far too much work. A smaller group of useful words can get the repeated speaking practice they actually need. 3. Try to Speak Before Looking Up the Word This is my favorite method from the video. Choose a topic and start speaking or writing before preparing all the vocabulary. Eventually, you reach a point where you know exactly what you want to say but do not know how to say it in Japanese. That missing word suddenly matters. Looking it up at that moment creates a much stronger memory than memorizing another random item from a list. 🔔 Another Idea I Loved: Your Japanese Does Not Need to Sound Like Everyone Else’s The last part of that video goes beyond vocabulary. Many learners want to sound perfectly “natural,” but there is no single version of natural Japanese. Age, job, personality, social group, interests, and life experience all affect how someone speaks. The Japanese you build also comes from everything you have watched, read, listened to, and studied. I really like the idea of choosing expressions that feel like something I would actually want to say , rather than trying to imitate an imaginary perfect Japanese speaker. That is one reason YUYU’s learning advice works for me. It is practical, but it also leaves room for your own personality. 💻 YouTube vs Spotify: Which One Do I Use? I use YouTube and Spotify for different purposes. I want to… I use Study with Japanese subtitles YouTube Shadow YUYU YouTube Watch facial expressions and delivery YouTube Replay short study sections YouTube Listen while commuting Spotify Get relaxed Japanese input Spotify Listen without turning it into a lesson Spotify YouTube: Better for Active Study YouTube is my first choice when I want to study. The combination of: on-camera YUYU + Japanese subtitles + useful learning topics makes it easy to move from normal listening into active practice. It is particularly good for shadowing because I can see how the sentence is delivered instead of only hearing the audio. Spotify: Better for Casual Listening Spotify is what I use when I simply want Japanese in my day. YUYU has mentioned on the podcast that the Spotify side will not necessarily mirror everything uploaded to YouTube. Without needing to appear on camera, he wants the audio podcast to feel more casual and show a more relaxed side of himself. That makes Spotify especially nice for commuting, walking, or listening before bed. 🎙️ How I Actually Study With YUYU I do not study every episode intensively. That is probably one reason I have managed to listen for several years. I use two modes depending on what I want from the episode. Mode 1: Casual Listening Most of the time, the goal is: topic → main message → useful expressions I listen while: commuting walking doing chores doing simple work sometimes before bed I do not pause for every unknown word. I do not look up everything. I try to stay with the speaker even when one small part is unclear. This type of extensive listening has helped me become much more comfortable with longer Japanese. Mode 2: Intensive Listening When an episode contains a section I really want to learn from, I usually take one to five minutes and work through it properly. Step What I Do 1. Listen Follow the topic without reading 2. Transcribe Write what I hear sentence by sentence 3. Check Compare with the transcript 4. Read aloud Follow the audio 3–5 times 5. Shadow Close the text and imitate YUYU 6. Listen again Return to meaning without the transcript Step 1. Listen Without the Text I first ask: What is the topic? What is YUYU trying to say? I do not begin by collecting unknown vocabulary. Step 2. Transcribe What I Hear I pause sentence by sentence and write down what I hear. When I hear the word but cannot remember the kanji, I write it in kana first. 🔔 My rule: this is listening practice, not a kanji test. Step 3. Check the Transcript I compare my version with the original and usually sort problems into three categories: I did not hear it correctly. I heard it, but I did not know the word. I knew the words, but I misunderstood the sentence. That tells me what actually went wrong. Then I mark useful vocabulary, readings, grammar, and expressions. Step 4. Read Along 3–5 Times I play the original audio and read aloud with YUYU. I focus on: pronunciation rhythm pauses new vocabulary sentence endings I do not want a new word to exist only as kanji in my notes. I want to recognize its sound immediately too. Step 5. Close the Text and Shadow Then I remove the transcript and shadow the audio. A section that repeatedly makes me stumble gets rewound and repeated. I do not keep moving forward while making the same mistake. Step 6. Listen Again for Meaning Finally, I listen again without the transcript. For a short section I have studied intensively, I want comprehension to feel close to complete by the end. Sometimes I also replay a familiar section at 1.25× or 1.5× speed as an extra processing challenge. 💛 Is YUYU’s Patreon Worth It? I eventually joined YUYU’s Patreon because I wanted to use the podcast more seriously for study. I paid for the membership myself and chose the ヘビーリスナー / Heavy Listener tier, which cost HKD 40 (about US$5) per month when I joined. Everything in this section is based on my own experience as a paying member. My verdict is straightforward: Casual listening: You do not need it. Intensive listening and shadowing: I think it is worth it. What I Use as a Heavy Listener Feature Why It Helps Me Podcast scripts Check exactly what I misheard Furigana versions Connect sound with written Japanese Vocabulary tables Less vocabulary prep Multilingual meanings Useful beyond Japanese-English lookup Shadowing website Easier structured practice Script archive Go back to older episodes The tier also includes regularly added podcast scripts, monthly topic requests, supporter credits, and access to a page for downloading podcast scripts. The Scripts Make Intensive Listening Much Easier The transcript is probably the part I use most. I can listen without text first and then check exactly where comprehension broke down. Did I fail to hear the sound? Did I hear it correctly but not know the vocabulary? Did I know every word but misunderstand the sentence? Having the original script makes those differences much easier to spot. The furigana version is especially useful when I recognize a sound but do not immediately know the kanji. I Really Like the Vocabulary Tables In the member materials I use, vocabulary is already organized into tables with readings and meanings, including multilingual support. I prefer this to a long unstructured word list. Without prepared materials, an intensive study session can start with a surprising amount of admin: find the transcript → check readings → look up vocabulary → organize notes → finally begin practicing The vocabulary tables remove part of that preparation. The Shadowing Website Is the Biggest Study Upgrade Heavy Listener members can also access a website designed for shadowing practice. That makes the membership much more valuable to me as a learner who actually wants to work with the audio. Instead of preparing everything from scratch, I can move through: listen → transcript → vocabulary → read aloud → shadow → listen again That is what I am really paying for: less preparation between finding an interesting episode and actually studying it. Is It Necessary? No. The free YUYU content is already excellent. I would not pay simply to continue listening. I pay because the membership makes active study much easier , and for that purpose I think the Heavy Listener tier is worth it. ⚠️ When YUYU May Not Be the Best Podcast for You YUYU is one of my favorites, but it is not the right starting point for every learner. You Are a Complete Beginner Twenty or thirty minutes of fairly natural Japanese can be exhausting when basic listening still requires heavy translation. A slower learner podcast gives you a better starting point. My Japanese podcasts by level guide includes easier options before moving up to YUYU. You Prefer Very Short Lessons YUYU works well for long-form listening, but it is not always the best choice when you want a five-minute lesson focused on one grammar point. For intensive practice, I solve this by choosing a short section instead of studying the whole episode. You Mainly Need Fast Multi-Person Conversation Most YUYU episodes train you to follow one person developing a topic. That is excellent for: listening stamina explanations opinions stories conversational phrasing It gives you less practice with: interruptions rapid turn-taking overlapping speech unexpected responses several different voices Dramas, interviews, native group podcasts, and actual conversations can fill that gap. 🔄 What to Listen to Before or After YUYU I see YUYU as a middle step rather than an endpoint. Your Situation What Makes Sense YUYU feels too difficult Start with slower learner podcasts YUYU feels just challenging enough Keep it as regular N3–N2 input YUYU feels very easy Add native podcasts, interviews, and dramas You want more options Browse my best Japanese podcasts for learners I would not rush to native podcasts just because YUYU becomes comfortable. There is still plenty to learn from how he organizes ideas, explains vocabulary, and uses conversational Japanese. But adding more unpredictable native content gradually helps close the remaining gap. ✅ Final Verdict After three or four years of listening, my YUYUの日本語Podcast review is still an easy five stars for intermediate learners. More importantly, it is one of the few Japanese-learning podcasts that has stayed in my routine for years. The reason is not one standout feature, but the way several things work together: natural speaking speed clear pronunciation teacher-style paraphrasing Japanese subtitles on many YouTube videos useful language-learning advice light but varied topics frequent updates a personality I genuinely enjoy listening to It is structured enough to study seriously but relaxed enough that I do not always feel like I am studying. ★★★★★ Highly recommended for N3–N2 learners. YUYU is especially good once slow learner Japanese starts feeling too controlled but native podcasts still require too much effort. For me, it has been one of the most useful bridge resources between the two. UYUの日本語Podcast Review FAQs What JLPT level is YUYUの日本語Podcast? I recommend it most for learners around N3–N2 .
